Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of unduly delaying the debate on the estimates of the Department of National Defence. However, I believe it is important at this time that I make a few observations and suggestions first in the interest of the department, and also in the interest of all those who take part in its formation.
When we look at the various items which make up these estimates, we realize, Mr. Chairman, that what has happened this year is exactly the same thing which we have criticized last year. Last year we requested a substantial reduction in the amounts earmarked for national defence whose estimates make up nearly half the total budget of Canada. It seems that our requests and protests have not been heeded because this year we find in the estimates exactly the same amount as last year. There have been some changes here and there, and a few amounts have been changed, some decreased, others increased, but when you look at the total amount for the Department of National Defence, you come to the conclusion that it is exactly the same as the amounts submitted to the house last year.
In other words, the national defence budget which is submitted to us this year is exactly the same as that submitted last year. I therefore come to the conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that it is an insult to the intelligence of Canadians and to the intelligence of the taxpayers. There have been no efforts to lower expenditures and to put an end to waste and extravagance, while various other countries of the free world were making some effort to

Supply-National Defence lower their expenditures on national defence and thereby alleviate the burden of their taxpayers. Surely, here in Canada, no way has yet been found to cut down on administrative expenditure, especially not in this department. England is reducing her budget. So are the United States. Other countries, which I will not mention, have done likewise.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, why Canada should not strive to reduce expenses to an amount much lower than that submitted to us last year and again this year. I recognize, Mr. Chairman, that we still have to face a potential enemy, who has no respect for peace nor freedom. I understand that we must remain on guard because of the behaviour of those conquerors from the Soviet union. But I believe that on looking at the international situation, as it is now and as it has been for some time already, we come to the conclusion that we are now engaged in a cold war, one still wanted by Russia, but which is waged on an economical basis. That is their change of attitude. It seems that Russia is trying today by all possible means to control the economic field and to invade markets hitherto under the exclusive control of democratic countries.
I would therefore urge, Mr. Chairman, that for the balance of this year and before the next estimates are tabled, an effort be made to reduce to some extent the expenditures of this department and, at the same time, as I have said, to lighten the Canadian taxpayer's burden, which is already too heavy.
I would go even further and suggest that an inquiry should be made as a result of the statement of General Guy Simonds and those of other high-ranking Canadian soldiers who are glad, today, to have recovered their freedom because it allows them to express their opinions. Even though this request was turned down in the house, the other day, I believe that an inquiry is urgently needed, so that the various military men who have occupied key posts at the head of our armed forces may testify and thereby throw some light on the various accusations and statements made since they left the Canadian Army.
National defence, Mr. Chairman, must not come to mean national expense. National defence must not be for the Canadian taxpayers a highway to ruin.
More than ever, the time has come when those who have to pay for the upkeep of this enormous defence budget should know exactly what use is being made of their taxes
[Mr. Dufresne.l

by this important department. At this point, Mr. Chairman, and in the light of the damning evidence of those who leave the services to reenter civilian life, it would seem that inefficiency, extravagance and waste are constantly on the increase throughout the department whose estimates are now under review.
I would like, in a few words, to give two examples. About two months ago, I had the privilege to take part on the C.B.C. French network, in a television program entitled 'Les idees en marche", where questions of national defence were being discussed. The topic we had to deal with on that particular program was whether our national defence was costing too much.
I do not wish to repeat what was said, one way or the other, on that program but I would point out that, at that time, I dealt with a particular point which, I believe, I should again bring up this morning.
Everyone of us knows that, in the province of Quebec, especially at Sorel, guns are being manufactured for the American as well as for the Canadian navy. It seems however- those are not my own conclusions but they are based on a report submitted to the cabinet by none other than Mr. Watson Sellar, Auditor General of Canada-that guns made in this country are costing Canada $112,000 more per unit than those exported to the United States.
Well, Mr. Chairman, it will be said, I know, that the planning, the assembly, the machinery, and some of the engineers who were responsible for the development of that unquestionably very useful gun, came from the other side of the 45th parallel.
I also realize that our neighbours to the south were doubtless put to some expense in getting this production under way. However, what is beyond my understanding is that the cost has been so heavy that Canada has had to pay $112,000 more per gun produced at home.
Let us imagine what this would amount to if, within a few years, hundreds, not to say thousands, of guns were so produced.
I believe-I am sure that this opinion is shared by all hon. members of this house- that it is a bit ridiculous to have to pay so high a price for something produced in this country when we are able to sell that same product to other countries, to our very neighbour, at a price which, in my estimation, is about a third, or 33J per cent cheaper.

I hope, Mr. Chairman, that inquiry will also be made into the production of these guns and that the department will give it all the attention it deserves so as to bring some measure of relief to the burdened Canadian taxpayer who has to foot all the bills.

Supply-National Defence (Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I come back to that expense which, it seems to me, is ridiculous, preposterous, unnecessary. Here are three servicemen whose sole duty is to look after a billy-goat. The corporal probably orders the two soldiers to curry it down in the morning, to wash it, to tidy up its headquarters and to summon the vet when required.
Mr. Chairman, to my mind, that amounts to downright waste.
Waste might seem funny to some hon. members but, after all, we must remember that the Canadian taxpayers are footing the bill for this waste, and that is why I protest at this time against this condition.
For those few reasons, Mr. Chairman, I repeat that a serious inquiry is absolutely necessary and that it should be carried out by people who, by no manner of means, would be interested in protecting those who are guilty of that waste of public moneys.
Coming back to my billy-goat, Mr. Chairman, there are sometimes complaints in the Quebec district that the advertisements appearing in the papers and inviting our fellow-citizens to enlist in the armed forces do not give the expected results. However, when a young man eager to make a career in the Canadian army, or wishing to spend some time in the army to learn a trade that will help him to earn a decent living later on, in business or industry, is told by the senior officer of the recruiting office that his work from now on will consist in looking after billy-goats, I do not think that that is one of the best ways to prepare his future.
That again, Mr. Chairman, is one of the serious reasons why that waste must be prevented. Instead of spending money on the upkeep of a mascot, of a billy-goat, it might have been better to keep in the reserve army some regiments that have brought glory to the whole of Canada in the past, and perhaps particularly to French Canada, such as the Quebec, Levis and Mont-magny regiments, reserve regiments which were the pride of our district.
Mr. Chairman, I have another matter to bring to the attention of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney). Quite often people complain, and possibly not without cause, that French-speaking Canadians do not care for positions that might be offered to them in the Canadian army, in the military profession. However French-speaking Canadians should get more attention from
[Mr. Dufresne.3
the department. Like Canadians of other racial origins, they are known for their ability, their efficiency, their loyalty, and most of them have one great qualification which is not to be found among their neighbours: they are thoroughly bilingual. There should be a higher percentage of French Canadians in high and responsible positions, and occupying ranks in keeping with those important positions.
If a new war were to break out there is no doubt that the services of a large number of well trained French-speaking officers would be needed and necessary. Their contribution would be, as in the past, most welcome. To promote the enlistment of Frenchspeaking Canadians we should promise them a fair deal and positions in keeping with their ability and their efficiency. That, I think, might be a still more concrete way of cementing national unity in Canada, that unity which is essential to harmony and good understanding between Canadians of different racial origins.
Mr. Chairman, before I sit down, may I suggest to the minister that, when there is a transfer from one military camp to another, an effort should be made, especially when the training laid down for the different French-speaking soldiers or servicemen is over, to send these people back to the locality they came from or, at least, to some place not too far removed from their homes.
I realize that when French-speaking Canadians from the province of Quebec are sent into Ontario, for instance, or to a western province, it is done with the best of intentions; it is a tremendous help to bilingualism, which is becoming extremely and increasingly important in Canada. The government is also to be congratulated for taking English-speaking people and moving them, in due time, to the old province of Quebec, so as to enable them to learn our mother tongue.
Yet, Mr. Chairman, when these people have stayed for a time in any province not their own, it would seem right to take the necessary steps to maintain a family spirit which is mainly to be found in our home province, so that it may actively survive.
I therefore ask the government to provide for the return of those servicemen nearer to their homes when they have completed their training.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to submit, Mr. Chairman. I hope they will be taken in the right spirit, because my sole

Now, if my hon. friend from Nicolet-Yamaska is free some week end, he might go to the citadel and find out for himself how much it costs to keep that billy goat.

One army informant said Meyer is accorded the same privileges as any other beer salesman. However, he is not invited to join officers in a drink in the mess-
That is very thoughtful.
-and as a rule he talks only with the messing officer.
The army decided not to bar Meyer from the brigade area. As far as the Canadian army is concerned, the source said Meyer has served out his prescribed sentence as a war criminal, and is a German civilian who happens to sell beer.
Meyer was convicted December 28, 1945, of inciting his troops to deny quarter to allied soldiers in the battle of Normandy, and of responsibility in the execution of 18 Canadian soldiers who had been taken prisoner.
I think anyone who doubts his responsibility has only to read the book "The Trial of Kurt Meyer" by Lieutenant Colonel B. J. S. Macdonald, O.B.E., Q.C., who was the official prosecutor of war trials on behalf of the Canadian government.
We know this man has served his sentence, but that does not alter the situation and I think we have to consider the sensibilities and feelings of the mothers and widows of Canadian veterans before we consider the sensibilities of a former war criminal. I bring this to the minister's attention because I have spoken to a number of people who are quite concerned about it and I would ask him if he would issue instructions to the commander of our brigade in Germany to have some other beer salesman deal with the Canadian army rather than Kurt Meyer.

Mr. Chairman, in the minister's fine survey of the debate which had occurred previously and which he made yesterday he referred to the remarks which had been made by various members of this house, including those by the hon. memher for York West. One strange thing about the minister's reply to the speech of the hon. member for York West was that he disregarded completely quotations placed on the record by the hon. member for York West from an article by Lieutenant General Guy Simonds. I think what the Minister of National Defence might have done on that occasion was to deal with the various charges. Of course he might say that those charges were not made by a member of this house and consequently he was not called upon to answer them. I grant that such a reply would be a palliative but it would not constitute a really satisfactory reply.
May I refer again to the quotations which the hon. member for York West put on the record and which were taken from Maclean's magazine of June 23, 1956. As I say, the
[Mr. Herridge.l
article is by Lieutenant General Guy Simonds, C.B., C.B.E., D.S.O., C.D., which I think would be enough to qualify any man'. I quote from the article:
Our organization for higher direction is designed, and operates to provide military excuses for political expedients rather than offering objective military advice and sound execution of realistic planning.
That to my mind is a very serious condemnation of the Department of National Defence. I am not saying that the present minister should assume full responsibility for that- he could not possibly do so-but it is the Department of National Defence as it now stands. I quote further from this article so the people in the country may know what this man is saying:
Whatever the intention in the minds of its designers, it is the opinion of the author that this expensive overhead is not evolving sound and objective defence policies.
Because of this cumbersome system of direction, the responsible military chiefs of the three armed services are denied an opportunity to confront those responsible for political decisions with objective military advice and alternatives upon which decision must be made. Senior civil servants can, by deliberate and unwarranted stalling, defeat the recommendations of the armed forces, even though those recommendations have been approved by the cabinet.
That is dreadfully serious.
The organization of the defence department as a whole is cumbersome and lacks flexibility. To operate effectively in a major crisis it would have to undergo radical changes which would paralyse efficient operation at a time when it should develop its highest efficiency.
The whole passage fills me with the deepest concern. Let me revert to that one sentence concerning which I made an interpolation.
Senior civil servants can, by deliberate and unwarranted stalling, defeat the recommendations of the armed forces, even though those recommendations have been approved by the cabinet.
There comes to my mind a most serious instance which occurred in the United States in 1948. Chiang Kai-shek was faced with his last chance of effectively throwing back his foes. In April 1948 the United States congress passed the China aid act of 1948 which provided for $1,250,000 worth of small arms and ammunition to be delivered to Chiang Kai-shek. The government of the United States were unable to check on whether those goods had been delivered until late in the year when on November 9, after all possible chance of using that China aid in throwing back the communist foe and stabilizing Chiang Kai-shek's position in China had passed, it was found that that material had not yet been delivered.
That indicates a most serious situation in the United States government, and from this

evidence right here it looks as though a somewhat analogous situation obtains in the government of Canada, especially in the Department of National Defence. No one in this house with any responsibility can pass by such a situation, and it becomes my duty, in spite of every kind of disinclination I may have to interfere in matters pertaining to defence in connection with which I have never had any experience except through my sons and brothers in world war II, to raise this matter and urge upon the minister the most serious consideration.
I should like to read to hon. members a statement which covers the whole continent of North America and the western world. This is another statement which cannot be disregarded. It is made by Dr. Louis F. Budenz, who is probably the greatest authority on communism and the communist high command on the American continent. At one time he was editor of the Daily Worker but he repented of his ways as a communist and became of great assistance to the United States in its effort to deal with the terrible situation which has developed and which threatens to drag the United States to utter destruction, and all the rest of us along with it. The publication in which this appeared is dated June, 1956, and the article reads:
Speaking before the Loyola College alumni association in Montreal recently, Dr. Budenz referred to peaceful co-existence as instalment plan suicide, stating:
"Unless those who are in charge of the governments of the so-called western world are able, very shortly, to turn back the course of the past 20 tragic years in our international history, we are writing the downfall of the entire non-Soviet governments. We are writing the second chapter in the achievement of the world Soviet dictatorship with the hammer and sickle over Ottawa and Washington before the next generation has expired."
Before the babies now being born get out of high school.
Describing the west's catastrophic losses in the cold war, Dr. Budenz warned "that some of the greatest victories of the Kremlin were won in the western world . . . Poland was not lost in Poland, it was lost in Washington, D.C., and at Yalta."
That is all I shall quote from a most terrifying article called "Instalment Plan Suicide". I am sure that every person who listens to that or reads that will realize that we are in one of the critical periods in the whole world's history. It affects us here and now, and particularly it affects our Department of National Defence which is charged with the responsibility of protecting us against the very evils which Dr. Budenz says are just rolling in upon us.
I have another document, and I think everybody in this house has a right to hear some excerpts from this document. It is the
Supply-National Defence June 15, 1956, issue of what is called the Economic Council Letter, published in the United States. The heading is "Shall Other Nations Tell us What to Do?" Some may ask, "Why bring in things about the United States?" It is quite clear that we are bound up with the United States inextricably in our defence, and consequently what affects them affects us immediately. Here are some quotations from that letter:
But in the past 40 years we have forgotten George Washington-have engaged in three foreign wars, no one of which had anything to do with vital American interests. Communism had to do with all those wars-and was the only victor.
That is just as true of Canada except for the fact that our vital interests were more eminently concerned because we were part of the British Empire. Another quotation:
We are faced in the near future with utter disaster-unless we resume control of our own destiny.
In 1945 American military materiel, estimated at 35 billions, was surreptitiously destroyed-a fact almost never referred to in press or radio. A dying President at Yalta ceded Soviet Russia large areas in Asia; and presently, through machinations in our state department, all China was lost to communism.
When the minister introduced his defence estimates he said something which this rather contradicts:
After three years of war in Korea, during which 30,000 American youth laid down their lives, and while our state department connived with the enemy, we made an ignominious peace. That peace lost face for America throughout Asia. It may lead to the communizing of all Asia.
In Germany we joined Russia in dismantling manufacturing plants, many of which were shipped to Russia, . . .
I hope that Canada had very little to do with this disastrous occurrence. From my own personal study, I can vouch for the truth of all of these statements made here, as far as I have been able to find the truth. This is another quotation:
President Truman forced the United Nations to partition Palestine-which lost us the good will of 400 million Moslems. At the present moment, barring a miracle, this will lead to the loss of the Middle East with its vast oil deposits, and the entry of Soviet influence into Africa. In Spain in 1946, we joined Soviet Russia in withdrawing ambassadors, thus isolating Spain.
I am not sure what we did in Canada, but that is what the United States did. Again:
Let's take a look at certain things in the United States. The same element that for a dozen years has made our foreign policy, in 1945 set up the United Nations. The American people weren't told then that the U.N. was to become a supergovernment, and was to shape our foreign policy. But that is just what has happened-at least so far as those behind the U.N. have been able to make it so.

Supply-National Defence
I believe that is absolutely true.
No longer is the stress in most schools, colleges and universities laid on loyalty to America: it is loyalty to internationalism, represented by the U.N. and its specialized agencies, that is preached. Literally millions of persons, especially students, are brought to New York and shepherded through the U.N. buildings. Our great national holiday, the fourth of July, is played down and United Nations Day is played up. Some of the big foundations are in on this.
I think a good many members of this house will reflect with considerable concern on the fact that in Ottawa on July 1, our great national holiday, you would have hardly thought that it was any different from, say, March 1, judging from the decorations that we had.
Why March 1?

Well, March 1 is a date quite a long way away from it. Where were the bands that might have performed? Where were the decorations along the streets? Where was the celebration we saw in our childhood every time Dominion day came along? That celebration just was not there. Why? Because it is the day of the United Nations that we are celebrating. You can see that what is being said here applies to Canada in no small degree. Let me give another quotation:
. . . the internationalists set up GATT (general agreement on tariffs and trade), which has functioned without any authority from Congress. The present administration is now trying to pass the OTC (organization for trade co-operation) bill, which would constitute a back-door recognition and officializing of GATT. So far has alien propaganda gone, that efforts by the economic council to interest manufacturing associations in certain states to protest against OTC have disclosed that some of the larger manufacturers in those states are in favour of it. So gradually the United States is losing trade to cheap foreign competitors. A wage of $1.76 an hour (the average American factory wage) cannot compete with 15-cent labour in Japan.
Pro-communist activity is being supported through the churches. Dr. J. B. Matthews stated that in 1952 three per cent of the Protestant ministers in the United States were members of communist fronts. So the left-wing press and radio saw that he was retired as director of research of the Senate permanent subcommittee on investigations.
The left wing press and radio-with whom behind them?-saw that he was retired as director of research of the Senate permanent subcommittee on investigations.
Here is another quotation:
Implanted right in the center of New York city is the U.N. headquarters. Many of those employed there by other nations are communist sympathizers; yet they have diplomatic status. They come and go in the United States as they please. They can even park their cars in violation of traffic regulations and thumb their noses at the police-and they do. . . .
TMr. Blackmore.]
The softened attitude of the administration, beginning with the Geneva conference a year ago, has cost us friendship and respect throughout the world. The Russian leaders after Geneva saw to it that iron curtain peoples understood they no longer had any hope of rescue by the United States. Had not Khrushchev, Bulganin and Eisenhower drunk vodka together-and martinis?
What a terrible blunder Geneva was. You may ask what this has to do with defence. It has everything to do with defence, because if we are selling this country down the river by the back door what is the use of shovelling billions of dollars through the Department of National Defence to protect it through the front door? Indications are that we are making quite a lot of progress in that direction, selling Canada down the river by the back door. I can back that up if I have the opportunity but I do not know whether I will take the occasion to do so this year. Here is another one:
Moreover, it is now expected that the general assembly of the United Nations will vote for the admission of red China, that red China which General MacArthur and several of his successors wanted to destroy and could have destroyed had it not been for that strange influence that has controlled the last three administrations.
I do not know whether or not that is true, but I heard the other day that at the recent empire conference of prime ministers the general idea was that we would work towards the recognition of red China. I hope that was not so. If it is so, it is a very serious matter. Unless we have some ulterior motive like trade, it means that as an empire we have lost our sense of right and wrong. Here is another quotation:
Why is it not possible for the United States, as long as it remains in the United Nations, to have delegates who are first and foremost for America?
How interesting that is. When they appoint delegates to go to the United Nations these people, every single one of them, are against the interests of the United States and congress appears to be unable to exercise any influence over the matter. Here is its next quotation: "The answer would seem to be that those back of the White House mean to force through the admission of red China."
The next quotation is:
Why has the present Republican administration, elected on a conservative American platform, become as internationalist and un-American as that of either Truman or Roosevelt, both of which in general placed American interests last?
That is a serious question. What causes these things to happen? We are coming to it after a while. We have already had reference to influence of some sort. What is that influence?

What has this to do with
Canada's defence?

We are right on defence, 100 per cent. Just as sure as you live, as I said a minute ago, there is no use pouring billions of dollars into the defence department if we know beforehand that the representatives of this nation are going to sell us to communism.
Defence on our home ground.

Of course. For example, suppose the representatives of this nation go and use their influence to get red China admitted to the United Nations. You would have 450 million additional communists in the United Nations to exercise control over the United Nations, an organization which is now under the control of communism.
Nonsense.

It is nonsense to those who do not know. My young friend just does not know. That is all. He just does not know. These matters are very important. Here is another quotation:
The Republican national committee, which dictates the policy of the Republican party, appears to be interested, not in available facts, which show that the American people are not internationalists, but in instructions handed to it from behind the scenes.
By whom, I interject? I continue:
It has acted on hunches. One major hunch has been that the only way to beat the Democratic party is to out new-deal the Democratic new dealers on foreign policy.
What has that got to do with Canada?
I am fighting for the defence of Canada. I happen to have some children and grandchildren growing up in this country and I do not want them under communism, whether my hon. friend does or not.
Let the Republicans fight their own campaign.
Never mind a lot of these cheap remarks.
Don't say the United Nations is controlled by communists.

Here is another important quotation:
Great numbers of Republicans stayed away from the polls in the congressional elections of 1954. In many mid-western districts, a third of the registered voters stayed home. Inquiry has disclosed that this was due to resentment at the administration's successfully blocking by a single vote the adoption of the Bricker amendment, and to the administration's going all out to destroy Senator McCarthy, an outstanding foe of communism and one of the ablest political campaigners the Republicans had.

Yet officials of the Republican national committee, including chairman Hall, have refused even to look at the work charts and studies of the Dunn survey in spite of the compliments his survey has received from congressmen, commentators and editorial writers.

-and passing on their instructions to the committee.

Who is it who can do that? For whom are they working? Why do they do it? Why does the government not know about it? Why does the Minister of National Defence not do something about it? All I am concerned about is that there are hidden forces in Canada and hidden forces in the United States.
I pointed out in my speeches of the day before yesterday and the day before that hidden forces have evidently been acting in support of the Bank of Canada and the Rowell-Sirois commission report to the detriment of the Canadian people and in the interests of alien people abroad. I do not think the conclusion can be successfully questioned.
I wish to quote a passage from the Ottawa Citizen of some days ago. I think everybody

Is it not strange? The government shut him up by the simple device of conveying to him that if he did not keep his mouth shut he would not have protection any more such as he now enjoys.

is,	whether he is Anglo-Saxon, Celt or alien, he would be shut up in a hurry. That is the information that everybody in Canada ought to know.

On no occasion did I (Gouzenko) ever say that I had new information which I did not already give to the Canadian government. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Churchill.
The hon. member wants to ask me a question, and I want to answer him.

I should like to ask the hon. member a question. Is he presenting his own view or the view of his party when he makes the very serious allegation that the United Nations organization, and I assume all its affiliated organizations, are controlled by communists.
I am speaking entirely for myself.

I always hesitate to take part in a debate on national defence. It is not because I do not feel qualified to do so or at least as qualified as other members, but the complexities of the subject are such that I never know just where to start or where to end. The purely military aspects of our defence have been, and must be, decided upon by those who are qualified through years of careful study in their particular field. They have received and studied detailed and intimate facts on which they have to base their decisions. These are .things which we, as members, cannot do unless we have the time, which we certainly have not got, to go into the subject as deeply as the officials responsible.
With regard to the actual amount of the estimates which we are asked to vote, the other day the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre seemed to indicate that there was something odd in the round numbers of the total estimates of national defence. I do not see anything odd in these figures at all. For the last several years my understanding of what the government has been doing, and I am sure that is the understanding of other members, was that in the light of the knowledge they had of the economy they allotted as much as they felt could safely and wisely be allotted to national defence, and tailored the other items to that over-all figure. After all, defence is the most important single thing we have to face in the country, and other things certainly ought to be tailored to that amount.

The degree of priority of the various items within the departmental estimates must also be determined in the same way. However, those are things, as I said, that require a great deal of information upon which to base any decision. I wish to move to a field in which I feel I can make a contribution to this debate, and that, generally speaking, is the two great radar lines that have been built in our north.
Before dealing with them, I want to call the attention of hon. members to some of the physical facts relating to our country. Canada is a country that is larger in territory than the United States and Alaska combined. The constituency which I represent comprises about 175,000 square miles right in the heart of this country, yet it lies in the southern half of Canada. I represent nearly two-thirds of the province of Manitoba, which lies to the south of the Northwest Territories. Churchill, on Hudson bay, our northern port, is just about the geographical centre of Canada. Now, that is an amazing thing, but if you look at the map you will realize how much of Canada lies to the north of that. In my constituency, which is really a fringe constituency with regard to population, there are somewhere in the neighbourhood of 60,000 people. There are more people there than in all the Northwest Territories and the Yukon combined. When you think of the large territory that has to be covered, and that is the area we must defend, you will see some of the problems that enter into it.
I might refer to the solution of one of those problems. Our aircraft industry, in this small nation of 16 million people, has had to develop one of the outstanding aircraft in operation today, the CF-100. The problems related to its development were due to the size of the country and the distance it has to travel. I do not know of any other comparable problem anywhere, and for the same reason we have now to develop the CF-105. These are the problems that we, a small people, have to meet, and I am very proud of the way they have been met in the past.
Speaking of this tremendous area that I have mentioned, we have lying in that area possibly the richest resources that any country ever had under its charge. We have not fully coped with that area. There are many reasons why we have not, and one of the chief reasons is the small population and the services that have to be built and developed before we can properly cope with it. But when people get up and glibly say we are not properly looking after the sovereignty of that area or that the Department of National Defence is lax in looking after the sovereignty of that area. I wish they would
Supply-National Defence take a look at the map, take into consideration some of the things I have said and try to realize the tremendous problems involved. The amount of money necessary to do these very large jobs has to be squeezed out of the economy which is developing, fortunately, at a very rapid rate. If we do not develop at that rapid rate it will make that defence job all the more difficult; so that if it is a battle of priorities between development, which fortunately does not come out of the estimates but does come out of the economy, and other developments and the protection of that economy, which has a valuable part to play in our everyday life, and the choosing of which has the higher priority, I have no doubt as to what the choice will be.
When faced with this problem some people have said that it is a waste of money; that this area cannot be defended. Well, let us suppose for a moment that it is a waste of money. I do not for a moment agree with that. I think it is a defensible area, or the people charged with those decisions would not have made them. I am leaving the military aspect for the moment. The country that those two lines run through is important; it is rich country; it is country that must be occupied by us as fast as we can occupy it or other people on this globe will occupy it in spite of us. The Canadian construction crews who have gone out and worked in the construction of those lines are getting a knowledge of their country that they never dreamed existed. They are finding out something about the country in which they are living and of which they are a part, and that will be of tremendous value in itself in making the rest of Canada aware of the lands within their borders.
There is only one regret I have in connection with the development of these lines and the development of the north that goes along with it, and that regret is that it has been the action of another country that has forced us to take the close look at our country that we have been taking. These lines will have a tremendous impact on our country in the future. Even if we admit they are not militarily worth while, every dollar spent there will be economically worth while because it will place an umbrella over the whole nation and it will assist tremendously in the prospecting, in the pioneering and in the developing of that northland.
I am afraid I have not given the picture as I should like to give it because it is such a large one to give. It is ridiculous to say that because our neighbours to the south are paying for the construction of the D.E.W. line, and are looking after the military aspect of it, we have lost our

Supply-National Defence sovereignty over it. The mid-Canada line runs along the 55th parallel, roughly, and I can remember in my school days hearing the slogan "54-40 or fight". We all know now how ridiculous that was and how ridiculous it is to say that the Americans are going to control us or have any influence on us that we ourselves do not agree to or recognize as being part of our geography or part of the facts of life that we live on their borders. Therefore, I feel that these fears are quite illogical and are only part of the general lack of knowledge that we as Canadians have of our own nation.
Now, as I said, it is true that many of our preparations may in the future prove to have been unnecessary-again I am speaking of military preparations. They might prove to have been unnecessary and I am sure that everyone here hopes that they will prove to have been unnecessary; but I cannot think of any military decision taken in the past that was unnecessary within the scope of the facts on which it was based.
There has never been such a time of uncertainty in our history, uncertainty as to what we should or should not be doing in many fields; but in the midst of that uncertainty I do not think we have ever been better served by those whom we have charged with the responsibility of our defence.

Mr. Chairman, first, I should like to comment on the speech made yesterday by the senior hon. member for Halifax, in which he sought to establish that there was not any need for the committee requested by the Leader of the Opposition because great masses of information in regard to defence had been provided. Now, I can only describe the speech of the senior hon. member for Halifax as a collection of half truths, inaccuracies and words which added up to complete misrepresentation of the facts of the situation. It is quite true, as the hon. member said, we have had a lot of information in regard to defence matters, but a great deal of that information was in regard to details which were not of very great importance and did not assist us very greatly in discovering what the real facts are in regard to our defence situation.
On the other hand, the information which would place us in the position of knowing to what extent our defence forces are efficient and effective and whether we are getting value for the large amounts of money which we are putting into defence-those facts have very frequently been denied to us.
The hon. member for Halifax said that as far as the opposition is concerned everything is wrong with defence. We constantly say,


"Everything is wrong with defence". Nobody on this side of the house has ever said everything was wrong with defence, or anything like that. We have throughout always been willing to admit and, as a matter of fact, to state that the officers and men in our defence forces are of high calibre, the morale is good and they have produced some efficient and effective units. The fact that we have made a considerable number of complaints in regard to the way in which the defence department has been carried on, and a great many criticisms on the general policy followed, and so forth, does not add up to saying that everything is wrong with defence. Nobody has ever maintained that everything was wrong with it.
I was particularly surprised that the hon. member for Halifax should have taken the proceedings before the defence expenditures committee of 1951, 1952 and 1953 as an example of the enormous amount of information on defence which was given to members on this side of the house, as an example of the fact that a defence committee such as that asked for by the Leader of the Opposition is not required. I think the hon. member showed a great deal of effrontery in even referring to the proceedings of the special committee on defence expenditure as an example of how much information was given to us. I have only one volume of the proceedings with me whereas I think the hon. member yesterday had the complete proceedings. If you go through the proceedings you will find instance after instance where information was denied to the members of that committee. In other words, rather than being an example, as the hon. member tried to indicate, of how much information was given it is a great example of exactly how much information was denied us.
It is true that a great deal of information was given to that committee but a vast portion of it was extremely irrelevant information. As a matter of fact, I believe the tactic pursued in that committee was an attempt to overwhelm the members of the committee with a tremendous number of figures and statistical lists of the number of pairs of socks on hand and things of that kind so that the committee would be bogged down in details and unable to obtain the information it desired.
When it came to requests for vital information, on the other hand, we were denied information. I will refer to only two instances which I think illustrate the point quite well. On April 29, 1952 at page 83 of the proceedings of the special committee on defence expenditure the following appears:
The chairman read the second report of the subcommittee on agenda, as follows:

Your sub-committee on agenda met on April 24 and 28, to consider the following notice of motion of Mr. Harkness, namely:
(a) That the Department of National Defence be asked to bring before the committee at its next meeting officials who can give us the general administrative set-up at Petawawa.
Then paragraphs (b), Cc>
and (d) are set out containing details of the particular witnesses we sought to have appear. Then it goes on to say:
Your sub-committee recommends that the above notice of motion be not entertained at the present time.

that the committee proceed with his motion as contained in the above report.
After debate, Mr. Applewhaite moved in amendment thereto
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
In other words, the entire motion for the production of witnesses and papers was struck out. That was voted on and of course my motion was voted down. The proposed amendment was carried and the committee was denied the right of calling witnesses and investigating what had occurred at Petawawa.
Mr. George S. Currie, of course, carried on an investigation subsequent to that which disclosed a number of facts which have never been very palatable to members on the government side of the house.
Another similar instance of denial of information occurs in the proceedings for June 12, 1952 as recorded at page 412 thereof. I was asking a series of questions and here is one which appears about one-third of the way down the page:

In connection with 87(a) which is the big item in this whole thing-
This was a list of the expenditures for equipment as far as the air force and army were concerned.
-being far more than all the rest of these items together, the note at the bottom says supplier includes A.V. Roe-CF-100, Canadair-F-86 Sabre I presume, and probably other aircraft. Now, could we be told that it is these two aircraft that the item takes in or whether there are other aircraft?
We then proceeded to discuss the matter of security which was brought up and the discussion continues for two or three pages. The net result was that we received no information whatever concerning that item which, as I say, was larger than all the other items put together. That is typical of the way in which that committee was conducted.
It is all very well to say that all kinds of information was given in this committee and in other ways, but the important point is that the information we obtained was a mass of minute details which were not important and the really important questions which
Supply-National Defence would have enabled us to obtain a picture of the situation were left unanswered and the information was denied us.
From this point I would go on to comment on the speech made by the minister yesterday and I think the same criticism applies to his speech. In other words, the minister answered some of the small specific questions which were brought up in considerable detail but he did not answer the general criticisms raised with regard to policy and organization and things of that nature. He simply did not answer the important questions which were posed in the speeches made by hon. members during the course of this debate.
The minister made an attempt to answer the statements or allegations or whatever you want to call them which are contained in the article written by General Simonds which appeared in Maclean's magazine and which has been referred to here so frequently. In connection with that I will just read an account of his remarks which appears in this morning's Gazette:
Mr. Campney said General Simonds' views are "merely expressions of opinion and not necessarily statements of fact."
Well, I think I could agree with that comment but I would say that the minister's remark also applies to the statements he made yesterday. In other words, he offered statements of opinion which were not necessarily statements of fact.
When it comes to statements of opinion concerning the subjects General Simonds dealt with in his article, I am more prepared to accept his opinion than the minister's. Having been the chief of staff and having spent his lifetime in the Canadian army, General Simonds I think is perhaps better qualified than is the minister to express an opinion as to the efficiency of Canadian defence headquarters. I think he is better qualified than is the minister to state an opinion as to whether defence headquarters could operate efficiently and effectively in the event of war.
In his statement yesterday the minister said he was convinced that national defence headquarters here was efficient and effective and would do a good job in the event of war. That was his opinion and that is all it is. The opinion of the minister is the complete opposite of the opinion expressed by General Simonds and I think the General's opinion on that subject is much more valid than is the minister's opinion.

Mr. Chairman, before the luncheon recess I had been commenting upon the reply made yesterday by the Minister of National Defence and had pointed out that while he had dealt with some of the smaller specific criticisms, such as the publication of books on hockey by the department, he had failed to deal with many of the more far-reaching and important criticisms by hon. members and also in magazine articles and other places by two high-ranking officers recently retired, General Simonds and General Macklin. I should like to ask the minister to deal specifically with some of the statements which appeared in the article by General Simonds in Maclean's magazine which have not been dealt with so far. They are summarized at the beginning of the article on page 22, and the following are three points which I do not think he touched upon:
1.	There is no co-ordinated effort to evolve a sound and comprehensive defence policy.
2.	The Canadian chiefs of staff committee is "packed" to protect the government against the receipt of unpalatable advice.
3.	Senior civil servants can, by deliberate and unwarranted stalling, defeat the recommendations of the armed forces even though those recommendations have been approved by the cabinet.
When I spoke on these estimates before I had gone into this matter of general policy or lack of general policy as far as defence is concerned and had asked the minister to say something about that. I had also in some detail gone into the necessity for a reorgani-ization of Canadian defence forces in view of the completely different circumstances which now exist owing to the development of thermonuclear weapons. In doing so I had paid some attention to the necessity, as far as the army was concerned, of developing more mobile and better protected forces which could operate in smaller units or forces where small units and sub-units could if necessary operate by themselves which undoubtedly would be necessary in the event of thermonuclear war. I also had something to say about the necessity for the unification of the armed forces and for a unified policy as far as all the forces are concerned, and the probable necessity, in order to accomplish that, of having an over-all chief of the defence forces as was found to be necessary during the second world war.
In the past few years since the war we have heard a considerable amount of talk about the integration of our three services. I am sorry to say that most of that talk I think has been eyewash. What it really comes down to is that the same branches of all three services as far as headquarters are


concerned are in the same building. All that that really has accomplished is to waste people's time because when the people in A branch of the army, we will say, want to talk to the people in G branch of the army, they must take a long walk to a different building. It is true that the people in A branch of the army, navy and air force are located in the same building, but I understand that they really have very little to do with one another. In other words, it shows some outward signs of integration but actually it does not accomplish that purpose.
In addition to that we have three tri-service colleges which are quite good as far as they go, for cadets that is. We have the defence college at Kingston which I think is a good institution and where you have people from all three services as well as from external affairs and I believe other departments attending as students. I think it is an extremely good institution. We have the same rates of pay in the three services, but apart from those things nothing else in the way of integration has been accomplished that is really of any value as far as I can see.
I think everyone admits that the old concept of sea power, land power and air power being separate entities having little or no connection with one another is now completely invalid. No one of those forms of military power is of any use or avail by itself. In other words, they are totally interdependent. However, very little if anything in the organization of Canada's defence forces has taken place to show that these facts have been realized and taken into account.
The second world war showed the necessity for singleness of command and direction at the top for all forces in each theatre of war. It was not until that singleness of command in each theatre of war had been put into operation that we secured victory in the last war. But in spite of this, when the reorganization of the Canadian forces took place after the war this principle of unity of planning and direction was disregarded, and it still is.
As one example, the army and the air force each operate separate staff colleges where different concepts and doctrines of war are taught. The navy has no staff college at all. I think it would accomplish a great deal more and be much more important to have tri-service staff colleges for the training of staff officers than it is to have triservice colleges for cadets. What was done to give some outward semblance of unity was really a clumsy and expensive attempt. A very large civil service was superimposed on the already extremely top-heavy staffs of the three services, duplicating the administrative machinery of the armed forces and thus

duplicating the cost and slowing down action with of course a consequent loss in efficiency. I think one might properly ask this question. If the quartermaster services of the forces are doing a proper job, why does all this work have to be done over again by civil servants? The thing seems to be completely without reason.
In my opinion the first step which should be taken as far as reorganizing Canada's defence set-up is concerned is the complete reorganization of national defence headquarters in order to secure efficiency and economy at that level. I have spoken on this subject before; perhaps it may be said that I have harped on it during the past seven or eight years. I have made speeches on the subject when the defence estimates were up going back to a period of two or three years after the war. In speeches I have made from that time on I have referred to the top-heavy organization at defence headquarters, and the large proportion of service personnel in administrative and desk jobs as compared to those in fighting units.
The former minister of national defence attempted to minimize this situation. At one time he produced some figures which purported to show that we were no worse off in this regard than the United Kingdom and the United States. I should like to point out that the worth of such figures depends upon what you take as fighting units. If you took the actual fighting units at the time mentioned and compared the number in them with the number in the services generally you would find the proportion to be very poor. The fact that we were very deficient in fighting units was shown up strongly when the Korean war broke out. We were not able to send a single battalion to the Korean war at that time. There was a terrible rush to recruit enough men to send one battalion, and about six months later we were able to send two more battalions. When the war came we did not have any troops to send, in spite of the fact that the minister kept assuring the house that we had adequate military forces to meet any foreseeable or likely contingency.
In any event it has been my contention for several years past that defence headquarters is top-heavy and as a result wasteful and inefficient. I now have two very powerful witnesses to reinforce that claim. General Simonds has said in this article that the headquarters is top-heavy. The minister, of course, said that was only his opinion. I think that that opinion is a very weighty one and it is reinforced by General Macklin and every other retired officer with any experience with whom I have ever spoken in
Supply-National Defence regard to the matter. General Simonds said that in a real crisis national defence headquarters would come to a grinding, shuddering halt. I claim that is probably correct, in spite of the minister's opinion to the contrary.
General Burns in his book on Canadian manpower, which was mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre yesterday, points out what a terrific waste of manpower there was in administrative jobs during the war, and he points out that, contrary to what the general opinion was, that wastage was greater in the Canadian army than in the United States army, which everyone was holding up as the greatest institution for providing ice cream for the troops and other services which were not too essential in getting soldiers on the field. Our wastage in administrative jobs was greater than in the United States army and considerably greater than in the United Kingdom army. That situation has continued in peace time. I am quite convinced that we are still wasting a terrific amount of manpower. This national defence headquarters is perhaps the prime example of this.
The situation there of the multiplication of staffs inevitably leads to waste of manpower and money and loss of time and efficiency. According to the Department of National Defence report for this year, there were 4,330 civilian staff here in Ottawa at the end of 1955. The number of service personnel at national defence headquarters was not given but it is very large, and as a matter of fact I should like the minister to give later the figures for the number of service personnel here at defence headquarters.
However, a few examples show the unnecessary duplication, triplication and qua-druplication of staffs. I would take as the first of these the medical services. There are three directorates of medical services, one for each service, and in addition a civilian advisory board. There is a brigadier or equivalent rank at the head of each of these services. As a matter of fact, at the moment I think the navy has a captain at the head of its service. I do not think there is any doubt that one directorate of medical services would be sufficient for the three services. There is no necessity to have one for the army, one for the navy and one for the air force.
When you look at the dental services you will find that there are not three directorates of dental services but only one, with a director at the head of it. The dental service looks after the army, the navy and the air force and does it very efficiently and effectively, as far as I can determine. There is

Supply-National Defence absolutely no reason why the same situation should not prevail as far as the medical services are concerned. The triplication of directors and their staffs there is completely unnecessary.
When we look at the chaplain services we see an even more ridiculous situation. Mr. Chairman, perhaps you could hardly credit it, but there are six directorates of chaplain services, each one headed by a colonel. There are six full colonels, and whom do they look after? According to this same report, at the end of 1955, there were only 246 chaplains, with these six directorates to run them. There is no doubt that two directorates, one for the Protestant and one for the Roman Catholic chaplains, for the three services would be ample, with two staffs instead of six staffs.
Another example is the directorate of military training in the army. When we look at the telephone book here we see that this directorate of military training has grown and flowered and has a multiplicity of full colonels as directors of various branches, each one with a considerable staff, each one with a G-2, majors, captains, lieutenants and goodness knows how many other personnel. We have a director of military training; we have a director of militia and cadets; we have a director of the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps; we have a director of the Royal Canadian Artillery; a director of the Signals; a director of the Royal Canadian Infantry Corps. In addition to that there are many other directorates of staff duties, military organization, planning and so forth, but the first ones I mentioned, the director of military training and these five directors for different corps, do the work that was done before the war by the director of military training and two staff officers.
It is admitted that the number of people in the army has increased very considerably, but I do not think there is any doubt that the increase has not been such as to warrant such a terrific multiplication of staffs as has taken place in these circumstances. The work of people of that kind consists to quite an extent of supervising training, putting out training pamphlets, issuing training directives and so on. The fact that we now have upwards of 50,000 people in the permanent army as compared with, say, 4,000 or 5,000 before the war, with a smaller number of people in the militia than before the war, does not warrant such an enormous multiplication of staffs, as far as training duties are concerned, as this shows.
As another example, each service has a personnel or manpower branch, and in addition to that there is another on the civilian side dealing with civilian personnel. In


other words, there are four personnel agencies or directorates, or whatever you wish to call them, all dealing with the question of manpower. One would be sufficient. Of course, one of the results of having these various personnel directorates is that you have recruiting stations for all three services in each province and each city of any size. When you walk down the street in most of our cities, you will see an R.C.A.F. recruiting station; somewhere else you will see an army recruiting station; and somewhere else you will see a naval recruiting station. In other words, there are three recruiting stations, each with a staff and each paying a high rent in the downtown parts of our cities, to do the job that one recruiting station could do for all services and perhaps do more effectively.
Another example is with regard to pay services. There is a separate pay service for the army, navy and the air force. One pay service could handle the whole thing quite readily.
These are just some of the examples of the duplication, triplication and quadruplication of staffs and of the effort that goes on at national defence headquarters and is multiplied right across the country. I should like to refer now to one of the criticisms General Simonds made and it is to be found at page 66 of Maclean's magazine for June 23. It reads in this way:
Power without responsibility is the theme that permeates the whole Canadian organization tor the higher direction and control of defence.
That is national defence headquarters, of course.
The Canadian chiefs of staff committee is "packed" to protect the government against the receipt of unpalatable advice, rather than present the military case objectively and fearlessly on its merits. The deputy minister of national defence, the permanent chairman, chiefs of staff and the chairman of the defence research board are all members of the chiefs of staff committee, yet none of these has any definite responsibility either to parliament on the one hand or for the end result as represented in the operational capability of each service on the other.

Mr. Chairman, I had decided not to take part in this debate and I would have preferred to continue to listen to the very interesting speeches coming from the other side of the house but as I heard a very silly speech delivered this morning by the member for Quebec West I thought an answer should be made to that speech. If the member for Quebec West was trying to get somebody's goat, he certainly put his own neck on the block. I have information given to me about the goat of

the 22nd regiment, and during the recess a few of my friends to whom I have spoken have asked me the same question: Why in heaven has the member for Quebec West picked on the glorious 22nd regiment to make a farce of it?
I have received information on the question of the goat. It comes from the department and I also have further information coming from newspapers. I shall only refer to two of them. The goat referred to by the member for Quebec West was presented by His Excellency the Governor General on behalf of Her Majesty the Queen to the Royal 22nd Regiment last October. I should like to see every member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition in his seat to listen to that and to take the matter more seriously than the member for Quebec West did when he was here. This goat was specially selected from a herd in the United Kingdom maintained by the crown. All the costs concerned- and this should be noted by every member of the house-in the upkeep of the goat are met from regimental funds. swallowed it yet? Then, there is an article in the Ottawa Journal of October 1955 which is headed, "Massey presents royal goat to famed royal 22nd". It reads:
Quebec, October 3:-The 1st battalion of the Royal 22nd regiment marched proudly along historic Grand Allee Saturday with a new mascot- a specially-trained goat presented to the Quebec army unit by Governor General Vincent Massey.
The parade was in the character of a farewell demonstration by the 800 men who embark here Tuesday-

Mr. Massey-
