speechtext: Order. The hon. member who has the floor may not be interrupted without his consent, as the hon. member well knows.
On a point of privilege- Mr. Chairman-
He is the mascot; he has certain privileges.
I am proud to be the mascot of a great party like mine.
What have you got on your horns?

Quiet, children. My question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, is that the hon. member for Portneuf just said, why should the hon. member for Quebec West pick on the 22nd regiment? Never at any time have I mentioned anything regarding the 22nd regiment. I am proud of this regiment and many of its members are in my constituency. I do want to tell the hon. member for Portneuf that he has to withdraw those words.
Oh, oh.
If I did pick on someone, I picked on the goat with all the expenses incurred. I am still sure the figures I gave were the right ones.
I would rather not withdraw, Mr. Chairman, because I have another epithet to replace the first one and my hon. friend will not like it. Shall I withdraw?
Do whatever you wish to do.
Shall I withdraw?
It is not up to me to decide; I am not the chairman.

I am positive- oh, I forgot one thing. He says he is proud to be the mascot of a great party. I wonder if it is reciprocal? I hope they get a leash and bring him back on the line.
I was really sorry to hear the hon. member this morning. Of course, he never thought-
You do not have to.

You do not have to think? Well, that is funny. He never thought that would be like a bouncing ball after the recess. I have read newspaper clippings from the Ottawa Journal, and surely he must believe in those if he believes in anything-I mean politically speaking.
What about the expense?
I gave the expense, $120, and it came from the personal funds of the N.C.O.'s and officers mess. Is that enough? Is that clear?
That is your own version.

It is my version and it is the version of all those who have been in the army. We must not forget, Mr. Chairman, that the-I will not say attack but I would say unhappy intervention of the hon. member for Quebec West about that goat is now a thing of the past, but I am sure the members of the "Van Doos" will not like it and will not forget it. When we are in the army and away from our families we must have something like this to keep up the esprit de corps, to enjoy ourselves
Supply-National Defence and to make the army more pleasant. That is normal; that is a tradition.
You should have a goat in your own ranks, too.

If we have to have one we shall choose it. Mr. Chairman, I think the matter of the goat is cleared up by the Ottawa Journal and by the information coming from the Department of National Defence. When the hon. member retires tonight and is on his knees with a good book in his hand dealing with the past, the present and the future of the Conservative party he will have time to meditate on what he did this morning.
Another thing he mentioned this morning was the Petawawa horses. On January 22, 1953, the hon. member for Hamilton West asked these questions in the house:
1.	Were any names of persons listed on Petawawa payrolls which did not represent living human beings?
2.	If so, how many?
3.	At what rate of pay were they listed?
4.	Was remuneration in cash or by cheque?
5.	If the latter, who cashed the cheques?
6.	Were deductions made for income tax purposes at source?
7.	If so, what claims, if any, were made for exemption because of (a) married status; (b) other dependents?
The Prime Minister answered that question as follows:
Mr. Speaker, as this question concerns matters in which the Department of National Defence, the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Justice are all three interested, I believe it would be appropriate that I answer it. The answer to the first question is "no" and therefore the remaining questions are not applicable.
You should read the Currie report.

I continue:
As this answer will appear to differ from a two-line statement in the Currie report tabled on December 15 last, I think I should state the facts in this connection so far as it has been possible to ascertain them.
It is very long, Mr. Chairman. I will not put it on Hansard. If the hon. member would like to consult my scrapbook he will find very interesting things in it-
I read the Currie report.
-pertaining to my hon. friend.
I read the revised one.

I continue:
The names on the payroll were the names of labourers who actually existed and who worked as teamsters. There were no false names on the payroll and no horses on the payroll.

Supply-National Defence
This question was settled long ago. After all, a majority of the Canadian electors settled it once and for all in 1953.

As an officer who served in the Welsh Fusiliers in the first war, I feel I must get into this discussion. I served from August 14 with the Welsh Fusiliers until I was knocked out, and actually any time a goat is mentioned it is a fighting word to the Welsh Fusiliers. I am sure the hon. member for Quebec West would not say what he said anywhere near the present members of that regiment. It is probably the oldest mascot in military history. It was adopted soon after the Crimean war. Queen Victoria gave the Welsh Fusiliers the first goat and, ever since that, as one goat dies it has been replaced from Windsor Great Park.
There is only one thing we have against the goat as a mascot and that is the smell. We have always arranged so that the dirtiest battalions and the dirtiest companies that have not been looking after their camps march immediately behind the goat. That was the punishment; and naturally they tried to do better the next time. While in France the goat got dirty and possibly did smell. Whenever a member of royalty made a visit to the regiment we would, in order to entertain him, have the goat in the mess and so we had two men wash and scrub all day to try to remove the smell of the goat, but, when royalty came in, it did smell.
I would suggest that these mascots are a wonderful incentive to the men. I know on long marches in France the colonel would turn around and say, "Damn you fellows, the goat can march, can't you?" And certainly the men would say, if the goat can do it, we can. Actually, we took a pride in the goat.
There are one or two matters I should like to mention while I am on my feet. My criticism of the Department of National Defence is their complete failure to assist rifle associations to get equipment. I have tried and tried through the present minister to get targets for a group in Penticton, a purely voluntary group of men-
Baa, baa!
We know where the goats are.

-who have purchased land areas suitable for target practice. All the members of the rifle association are young men. Some belong to local military units, and there are others, and they are anxious to be prepared in case of an emergency. We have the experience of the last war of the Pacific coast rangers who drilled themselves and conducted themselves in such a way that they could be of use in the event of an invasion of
[Mr. Gauthier (Portneuf) .1

the Pacific coast. The government appreciated the excellent work they did on a voluntary basis. This rifle association is willing to do the same thing. I am making a request of the minister. They were turned down completely. These targets are available. I believe some of them are at Armstrong and at the rifle range at Vernon. The department has condemned the range at Vernon; the targets are not being used. They are left to rust. They could be used by these people and they would use them if they had them. The department would be getting something for nothing. These young men are willing to train themselves to be of service to the department should the occasion arise. I hope the minister will change his attitude and go out of his way to help these men.
There is one other thing I should like to mention. I hold in my hand a copy of Roundel. I think the minister is probably aware of what it is. It shows a tight formation of jet aircraft. I am going to suggest that a tight formation of jet aircraft or of any aircraft is a real folly; it endangers life and makes useless a lot of our equipment in the form of jet planes. I do not have to refer to the accidents that took place in France where these jets were flying 500 or 600 miles an hour, or whatever rate they go, wing-tip to wing-tip. They are subject to human error; they are subject to mechanical error and all the errors that follow the mechanical age; and yet we take this unnecessary risk with our equipment, and more so with valuable trained pilots and others who may be on the planes. I think it is time the department called a halt to these tight formations. They are very pretty, we love watching them; they are really spectacular but they are highly dangerous. In a war, if you flew planes in tight formations like that it would be an ideal target for the enemy. The only way to fly in war is to scatter the planes as far as possible and your ground troops and your air troops to make the target as hard to hit as possible. In view of the impractical use of tight formations in war, I would suggest to the minister that it should be discontinued in peace to give those young pilots a break.

Mr. Chairman, I have to go to the banking committee in a minute. I know you are going to start questions pretty soon. I have one that I want to leave with the Minister of National Defence which I hope he will not find too tough. First I want to congratulate him in that he has handled the problem with which he deals better than they did in Britain where they had the famous battle of the bloomers which has just been concluded.
I notice in the latest annual report of the Department of National Defence they are now

giving a monthly clothing allowance for uniforms to the personnel of the armed services and I observe that the women receive $2 a month more than the men. My question to the minister is this. I hope he is not going to run into trouble with the Minister of Labour in view of his new bill concerning equal pay for equal work for women. I also hope he is not going to embarrass the hon. member for Hamilton West who for so many years has been asking for equal pay for women in that this is not going to degenerate into a policy of extra pay for women.
Very clever.

Mr. Chairman, in the last few minutes this debate has been a strange one in that we have gone from goats to bloomers. We have had an explanation as to the expenses incurred over the goat mascot of the "Van Doos" and we found out that the trouble with the Tory party is that they have too many mascots and not enough party.
Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, the senior member for Halifax, as he does on occasion, set himself up as the hatchet man for the government and said that the committee on defence expenditures which sat for about two years or more found absolutely nothing wrong with the department and that the opposition was extremely disappointed because they were unable to verify any of the charges that had been made concerning the Department of Defence Production.
I would like to remind the hon. member for Halifax that his memory must be pretty short. Surely he has not forgotten all the evidence that was brought out in that committee with regard to Penhold, Cold Lake, Namao and the other defence construction enterprises. Surely he has not forgotten the price of $13,258 a well that was paid to drill the wells at Penhold. One of them was 105 feet deep and cost something over $100 a foot.
Surely he has not forgotten the $664,000 in change orders that came about as a result of changes in decisions and so on after the contracts had been let. Surely he has not forgotten the $28,200 speed-up payment that was given to the major construction company engaged there because they were lagging in the time element of their contract. At the same time, during that speed-up period when they had asked for an expansion because they were unable to live up to the time limit the company was given another $4,900,000 contract at Cold Lake.
Surely he has not forgotten the $5,000 that was given to the contractor in order to pick up the cement slabs that were apparently covered by snow when the tenderer went 67509-392
Supply-National Defence there to make the tenders in spite of the fact that the tender definitely states that the tenderer has investigated into the circumstances, has looked over the site and is basing his tender on that ground.
I am not going to say anything more about that because those are things that could probably happen in any department of any government; but for the hon. member to stand up and say we were unable to discover anything wrong in that committee is surely folly.
How well I recall that when speaking in the debate after the committee had finished sitting the hon. member said almost tearfully that he had not heard any of the charges in committee that were being made on the floor of the house. The fact remains that we could not make any charges in committee because every time we opened our mouths to say anything the hon. member for Halifax would get up and say, "Mr. Chairman, I object. The hon. member is making a statement, he is not asking a question".
The very fact that immediately following the debate that took place the committee was closed off and has not been able to reconvene again is the best indication I know of that we must have found out something. That committee did a wonderful job. We touched upon only one phase of defence contracts. We should have been allowed to go on because I think the government gained a good deal as a result of the probing that was done in that committee.
I am not going to speak about that any further except to mention that the hon. member told us yesterday how much information the members of this house were allowed to receive here in the house and he pointed out that we could go anywhere at any time and go aboard any ship or enter any defence establishment. He took great pains to point out that even the public was allowed to go on board these ships and enter these establishments at fixed times. All I can gather from that comment is that the hon. member was trying to tell the public of Canada that their members of parliament are entitled to have exactly the same kind of information as is the public. Unless we as members of parliament have the opportunity of digging in and thoroughly investigating all phases of national defence we cannot possibly do the job we were sent down here to do.
After all, that department of government is spending more money than any other department, about $2J billion of the taxpayers' money. Surely to goodness we should be given practically all the information we want

Supply-National Defence concerning these expenditures so we can determine whether or not the money is being spent in a proper way.
We want to find out whether or not there has been any waste or extravagance. I am not accusing anybody of any crooked dealings or anything of the sort but I do think the attitude the government has taken, that it is almost a sacrilege to question anything having to do with defence, is wrong. We have a duty to investigate these things and I think we should be allowed to do so.
I have two more points to draw to the attention of the minister, one of which I brought up last year, and that is the question of ground to air guided missiles. Apparently the department has practically given up any idea of proceeding with an investigation in this field. I would like to point out to the minister that ground to air guided missiles working in conjunction with the radar lines could be of the greatest assistance in protecting this country against air attacks because these missiles would be ready in advance bases in the north long before any alert could be answered by any of our aircraft. They would serve as the first line of defence against any air attack coming from behind the iron curtain across the polar wastes.
I urge the minister to give serious consideration to this point. I know of no cheaper and more effective way of protecting ourselves against possible air attacks.
My last point is one about which I feel very strongly and although I mentioned it to the minister last year he did not deal with it at all. I have no doubt the minister will remember that I asked him what the possibility was of asking the press to withhold news of air crashes and military fatal accidents until such time as the next of kin have been notified. Time and time again throughout the years you hear the same old story that so many men of the armed forces were killed and that the names are being withheld until the next of kin have been notified. I cannot think of anything that would be harder to bear than for the people back home to have to sit and wonder if their boy or father is the one who has been killed. I would not want to have to sit by and wait until it was published in the newspapers.
I am not asking for the forcible suppression of news or anything like that, but I suggest to the minister that he ask the press to co-operate in this. I think the newspapers and radio bureaux of this country are humane enough to want to ease the suffering that would come about as a result of publishing that type of news. I have never been placed


in this position, but no doubt many hon. members have. No doubt they have had to sit back and wait for 24 or 36 hours after someone had been killed at a station and not be able to learn if it was their son. A wife should not have to suffer when her husband is on such a station until the news is finally published in the newspaper or over the air.
I put this to the minister in all seriousness, as I think a severe strain is placed on these people by having to wait for definite news as to who has been involved in a fatal accident.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to preface my brief remarks by saying that I am going to ask a number of questions which I do not expect the minister to answer at the moment. I had expected to ask these questions on the particular items, but unfortunately I must leave the house and will not have that opportunity. I shall ask the questions now and possibly the minister will answer them later on.
When the debate on the estimates of this department opened some time ago I asked a number of questions. In his remarks yesterday the minister answered some but not all of those questions. It may just be my interpretation, but to me the minister's answers were somewhat evasive; therefore I intend to ask the questions again.
First of all with respect to the cruiser Quebec, yesterday the minister stated that the Quebec has now been placed in reserve. I am glad to hear that, because a cruiser is an expensive ship to operate. I understand that the cruiser Ontario is being converted for the training of junior officers at sea. I should like to know the normal complement of officers and men on H.M.C.S. Ontario and what is the annual cost of maintaining and operating this ship.
Yesterday the minister said that one reason the Quebec was being put in reserve was that a sufficient number of other ships are now available for training. It would seem to me that since we are going to have an antisubmarine destroyer navy it would be much better to train junior officers on destroyers or similar types of ships rather than on a cruiser, which in all likelihood will never be used and which is most expensive to maintain.
The next thing I should like to deal with briefly is the destroyer escorts. I do not think the information given by the minister is definite enough, and I should like to know how long it will be before the St. Laurent class of destroyer and the Crescent destroyer escort will be in service and what the cost of these ships is expected to be. My understanding is that the cost of the prototype of this class, namely H.M.C.S. St. Laurent, was

nearly $18 million. Naturally it costs more to produce a prototype, but I should like to know if the other units of this class will cost less, the same or more per unit.
I should like to ask one question in connection with the Crescent and Tribal class destroyers which are being converted. Yesterday the minister told us that the cost of conversion and refitting will run to $4 million in the case of the Crescent class and $5,500,000 in the case of the Tribal class. He stated also that the life expectancy of these ships is something over 20 years, and this is also the case with the frigates. I should like to know the life expectancy of both the Tribal and Cresent class destroyers after being converted and refitted. Will it be five years, ten years or what? I expect that the minister will be able to give us that information, and also information with respect to the original construction date of these ships.
I think it is quite important to know how long these ships are going to be in use after we have spent $4 million refitting one class and $5,500,000 refitting another class. I should like to know the original cost of the Tribal class destroyer and also the Crescent class.
I have some questions that have to do with frigates, of which we apparently have about 20 in the Canadian navy. I believe there are 10 in operation, 3 on loan to Norway, 6 in reserve and 5 undergoing conversion. Yesterday the minister told us that the cost of conversion was approximately $3,500,000. I should like to know if any of these frigates were built after the end of world war II, or were they all constructed during world war II? What will be the life expectancy of these frigates after this rather expensive conversion job? I may be wrong and I hope the minister will correct me if I am, but I believe the life expectancy is about three or four years after this conversion which will cost about $3,500,000. I should like to know the original cost of these frigates and when they were first built. Unless my memory serves me poorly, it is costing a great deal more to convert them than it did to build them in the first place. It may be that I am mistaken, and I have no doubt the minister will give us the figures.
I asked earlier what type of engines these ships have. I do not expect the minister to give the details because naturally that information is classified, but I would like to know whether they are fitted with turbine or reciprocating engines? I do not think it would be out of line to ask if these ships are capable of overtaking a modern Russian submarine. My understanding is that a Russian submarine can travel at the rate of 25 knots under water, and I understood that 67509-392J
Supply-National Defence these frigates were not capable of that speed. It may be that alterations are being made to bring up the speed of these ships to equal that of Russian submarines. I would certainly be delighted to hear that was so. That is another matter which I hope the minister will clear up.
I know these are questions which are in the minds of the Canadian people and of those who were formerly connected with the naval services. In my opinion they are of great importance.
There is only one other question I should like to ask in regard to the matter of frigates. If these frigates are being reconverted at a cost of $3J million each and they cannot carry out the task of overtaking potential enemy submarines, I should like to know just what is the purpose of having them in the naval service and particularly of spending all this money on them. I understand that the general view, not only in this country but elsewhere, is that the new St. Laurent class destroyers are probably the most up to date and efficient type of antisubmarine vessels at present afloat, and I am glad to hear we are going to have a number of these; I believe it is 14. That is excellent, and they should make our antisubmarine navy, at least in quality if not in quantity, the finest afloat. But the thought occurs to me, what is the purpose of spending all this money on reconverting these frigates if they are not going to be used for any great length of time and if they are not capable of overtaking potential enemy submarines? I shall be delighted to read the minister's answers when he gives them.
If their speed is presently sufficient to enable them to overtake an enemy submarine, that is fine; and if they are going to have a considerable life expectancy I think the cost would be justified. Otherwise I think it would not. It has been suggested to me that these frigates are just a temporary stopgap until all the new St. Laurent class destroyers are built. If that is the case possibly the expense might be justified, but unless they are capable of catching an enemy submarine I still do not think it would be.

Before the first item is carried there are two or three questions I should like to ask and a few remarks I should like to make. I do not intend to go into all the ramifications of the Department of National Defence.
I said the other night that because of all the far-reaching angles of national defence-for example, the D.E.W. line is so far away that Canadians are not able to see just what they are getting for their

Supply-National Defence defence dollar-of all the dollars that are spent we have actually less to show for those spent on national defence, and that is partly because aircraft particularly and defence items in general become obsolete about the time when they go into production. Consequently it is an expensive operation.
Ever since the earliest days the city of London has been a military headquarters. Western Ontario and the city of London particularly, to put it mildly, were very much disappointed when the minister announced the disbandment of 420 squadron. With the changed flying conditions I do not suppose we could expect these things to continue indefinitely, but I think the city and I myself felt that here was a group of men giving time to the 420 auxiliary squadron.
I read very carefully the minister's reply yesterday to my question of the day before on what the plans were to use these personnel of 420 auxiliary squadron. I think that what actually will happen is that many of these men will be disappointed. They were going there in their spare time and flying those planes, but they are going to say that they are not interested in ground work and will give it up, not all of them but a great many of them. I was, shall I say, shocked to read in today's Montreal Gazette these words:
Montreal's week-end pilots in the R.C.A.F. are on the job full time this week and next.
It says that the two auxiliary squadrons, 401 city of Westmount and 438 city of Montreal will be equipped with Sabre jets and T-33 trainers, and each squadron will retain two propeller-driven Harvards. At the very time they are washing out 420 squadron, there in Montreal apparently they are equipping the squadrons with better equipment. The minister more or less says-perhaps he does not say it in so many words but he indicates by his actions-that it was an obsolete operation in London. Yet I find that in Montreal two of these auxiliary squadrons are being retained and equipped with better aircraft.
I think I suggested earlier that the minister should consider using 420 squadron personnel at London for transport and duties of that type. I know the minister will correct me if I am wrong, but I understand that there is a shortage of heavy duty transport facilities, both civilian and military, in Canada, This is a use that could be made of the airport facilities and the personnel there, and they would be flying the type of aircraft with which they are familiar. It seems to me that better use could be made of the knowledge these auxiliary squadrons have. I could not quite follow the minister.
[Mr. White (Middlesex East) .1
I understand that the disbandment order on the Hamilton squadron was lifted but not the one on 420 squadron at London. They are not going to be treated alike.
The ban has not been lifted on flying for 424 squadron.
Then I understand that both squadrons will be treated in the same manner?
That is my understanding also.

A question
was asked this morning about the brief submitted to the Minister of Transport by the Canadian airline pilots' association. I hope the minister will not interrupt and say that this is a transport matter, because I have just one reference to make. In their presentation regarding transportation they have this to say:
. . . there is a grave deficiency in Canadian air transport capacity and that there is no plan to meet Canadian responsibilities in an emergency.
That is not the first reference I have seen regarding the need for transport aircraft. In this modern age we need practically an airborne army, in my estimation, to move troops quickly from place to place. This is the very type of work that I think this auxiliary squadron could assist in doing. It could train men for that very purpose.
I am not going to burden the minister and the house with the entire contents of these two resolutions. I hold in my hand a resolution from the city of London regarding 420 squadron and toward the conclusion it says:
Therefore be it resolved that the council of the corporation of the city of London petition the dominion government, through the Minister of National Defence, to give serious consideration to the retention of the London airport as a flying station and that if it is impossible to retain No. 420 city of London squadron, another flying training unit be located at the London airport.
Later they suggest that a transport training unit be established at London if the present 420 squadron is not to be retained. I do not know what else I can add except to say, as I did at the beginning, that the city of London all down through history has been connected with national defence as a headquarters for military operations, and the citizens of the area rather feel that they are being let down at this time.
I have a couple of other questions I should like to address to the minister. I notice on pages 312, 321 and 334 of the details certain expenditures for fire-fighters in the armed forces. On page 312 there is an item of $1,405,040 for Are-fighters in the navy. On page 321 there is an item of $926,660 for firefighters in the army and on page 334 there

is an item of $437,360 for fire-fighters in the air force. These items total $2,769,060. That seems to me to be a terrific fire insurance policy to pay. The number of men are listed. How many fires have there been in each of the last five years in military establishments in Canada and what was the amount of the loss in each of the fires?

Mr. Chairman, I think the general debate is fast drawing to a close. I wonder whether the minister could clear up one or two of the questions which have already been asked before we proceed with the details.

Mr. Chairman, I have followed the debate with a good deal of interest and have received a good deal of advice on things past, present and to come, and even some advice on other departments, but I do thank hon. members for their observations.
Do you think you will profit by them?

I also thank them for their attention to this subject, which we all agree is of very great moment to all of us. There are a few matters I could deal with now. I know that a considerable number of matters will come up on the detailed estimates for the different branches, but there are a few subjects that I could possibly deal with now before we proceed with the consideration of the details of the estimates.
Yesterday the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich made a remark about the difference between the chiefs of staffs committees in Great Britain and Canada. I must agree that he extended my remarks to complete their accuracy, and I appreciate that. He also asked a question about the stockpiling of CF-100 aircraft and made some further remarks leading from that. I should point out that we do not have and probably will not have a stockpile of CF-100 aircraft in any permament sense of that word, because the rate of production is being reduced, as the hon. gentleman knows, and out of the rate of production as it now stands plus accumulated CF-lOO's our requirements will be to replace CF-lOO's in the four squadrons of the first Canadian air division in Europe, which has already been announced, to provide CF-lOO's for the three additional interceptor squadrons for air defence in Canada, which I have already announced, and to have a continuing bank for normal aircraft attrition and for spares.
Indeed, the CF-100 program is now ready to be phased into the development and, we hope, production of the CF-105. Therefore in effect we will not have, looking into the
Supply-National Defence future, a stockpile of CF-lOO's surplus to our requirements. That does not mean, of course, that they could not be produced if other nations of NATO wish to acquire them.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre asked for an explanation of the decrease of $24 million in the army estimates for this year. He was as usual apprehensive for the welfare of the army, and wondered whether this indicated a trend or a decision to reduce the army's status or its equipment. This decrease, I may tell him, is almost wholly attributable to the fact that the stockpiling of certain ammunition and vehicles has been largely completed, and that stockpiling involved large sums.
He also asked for further information about the additional armoured regiments to which I referred on June 20. There are a number of matters still being reviewed in that regard, and I am not in a position to give details about particular regiments. However, I can say that the intention is that the armoured regiments will normally be brigaded in brigade groups of all arms within the division and it will be possible, should the need arise, to use all the armoured regiments in combination after the manner of an armoured brigade as well as separately with the brigade group. That is part of the flexibility that we are trying to achieve.
I should like to assure him and also the hon. member for Calgary North that I think it is fair to say, and I am glad to note that some other members did say it, including the Leader of the Opposition, that our army, navy and air force are in first class fighting condition. I would not ask hon. members to take my word alone for that, but we have had the repeated assurances of General Gruenther and Sir Richard Gale, who has commanded our armed forces in Europe, with regard to the Canadian brigade in Europe. Other NATO commanders have spoken very highly of the fitness and capability of our brigade and air division as well.
I might mention in that connection that I find it a little difficult sometimes to reconcile the fact that we do listen to eulogistic remarks from members opposite with respect to our armed services and at the same time considerable criticisms of the department as such. Eulogistic remarks with respect to the service should be, and I think are, the principal test of the effectiveness of the department itself and of its whole organization. But I would not want the impression to go abroad that the end product is good but that the method of achieving it is bad. I do not think that adds up too well.
The hon. member for Brandon-Souris, in speaking about the auxiliary air force in

Supply-National Defence which he has such a continuing and deep interest, referred to the way in which the auxiliary force had been dealt with by the Royal Canadian Air Force as being arbitrary, high-handed and without previous consultation. I should like to say that before any decisions were taken with respect to the auxiliary air force the matter was given very careful study and consideration by the planning officers of the air force, and some months ago we brought in all the senior officers of all the auxiliary squadrons, had a long conference here in Ottawa and explained our problem and studied theirs. Since then we have endeavoured to the best of our ability to make sure there was not any arbitrary action taken or any decisions made without the ground for them being well known and appreciated.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, in his philosophic discussion yesterday which was very enjoyable, mentioned that probably the main usefulness of the early warning radar lines is to enable the strategic air command of the United States to get off the ground. I do not dispute that that is the principal reason, but I should like to keep along with that in the public mind the other subsidiary aims which are of very considerable importance. A secondary deterrent purpose of this line is to alert our defence forces so they may, in turn, counterattack the attacking forces. This may blunt any attack that may be made. We know-I think the percentage is correct-in the German bombing raids in the second world war that when the losses got up to something like 15 per cent of their planes the bombing raids practically ceased. The fact that we have this line and the fact that we would be enabled, we hope, to inflict great losses on any attacking forces, must have a deterrent effect on the plans of any potential enemy.
The other secondary object of the radar line is to alert the civilian population and the civil defence authorities.
I notice the hon. member for Kamloops is not here, so I shall not attempt to add to his confusion about the three ammunition depots at Kamloops and the two fire brigades, but I will be able to work the situation out with him. As a matter of fact it is under consideration, and I had hoped to have a detailed answer.
He is attending another committee this afternoon.

Yes, I understand that. The hon. member for New Westminster gave some figures yesterday. I had no advance notice of them, but I have asked to have them looked into. We try to keep the pay for our civilians in line with the going rates in
IMr. Campney.]
their locality. It may be that, although that is the target toward which we strive, in some cases we fall behind before picking up the slack. On the other hand I notice we have not had much trouble getting all the people we want. They seem to regard our service as not too bad.
A little while ago the hon. member for Calgary North referred to the number of civilians at defence headquarters, and asked for the number of service officers and other ranks there. The total figure for service officers and other ranks at national headquarters is 2,845, comprising 1,657 officers and 1,188 other ranks. I should like to observe in that connection, because I noted his critical remarks about headquarters, that, after all, headquarters does have to look after not only the 116,000 to 117,000 service personnel and the 54,000 civilians, but they also have the reserve forces of some 56,000 in the three services; a ground observer corps of over 80,000, and over 100,000 cadets. Altogether, therefore, in our many activities there are more than a quarter of a million persons being supervised by headquarters, and that requires a substantially larger staff than one might have if there were just the regular forces. We must also recognize that it would be a very poor attempt at economy, shall I say, if we were to try to make small savings at headquarters to the detriment of this vast number of people we have to oversee.
With reference to his remarks about triservice activities, I can assure him I recognize some of the points he has mentioned and we are trying and are succeeding rather slowly, perhaps, to get improvement in triservice activities. I think it is generally recognized now that the tri-service principle is a good principle. Events are probably pointing more and more to the principle, but we have to assimilate changes as we make them.
The hon. member for Calgary North, who has served in one of the services, knows that if you want to get full support of the services they have to be convinced that any change is in their own best interests as well as in the best interests of defence. I am not pessimistic in my feelings about tri-service development. I noted his suggestions with respect to certain specific cases which he thought should be expedited. We are working on one or two phases at the moment, and we shall continue to work on them. I hope we will achieve some results.

Since the minister is answering questions, will he answer my question regarding the armoured personnel carrier? Is it a figment of the imagination, or is it on the drawing board, or is it in production?

I made inquiries about this and I have not a detailed or final statement, but I think it is approaching the prototype stage. Work has been progressing on it for some time.
While I am on my feet there is another matter in which I know the hon. member is interested, because he mentioned it last year. He expressed the view that we ought to have a one-volume history of world war I. Now that the editing and writing of the second world war history is practically complete, I have given instructions to Colonel Stacey to prepare a one-volume history of world war 1.
I had a speech ready on that, so I shall file it away.
I was called to the phone for a minute and unfortunately did not hear the minister's reply to the questions. Did the minister reply to the question I raised this morning?
No, I have not as yet.

There is one matter I should like to mention in this debate and draw to the minister's attention, and that is the equipping and dressing of cadets throughout Canada. I bring this up because I have received a letter from the principal of the high school in Kincardine. It is a very short letter, and I should like to read it:
Almost every high school in Ontario which has a cadet corps is experiencing the same problem as we are in the Kincardine district high school. Each cadet corps is assigned a quota of cadets and all equipment is issued on the basis of this quota. The assignment quota is very frequently slightly higher than half of the number of boys in the school. Thus it is difficult to outfit and equip all the boys who take the cadet training.
For instance, in the Kincardine district high school we have 108 boys, while our cadet quota is 67. Thus you see that our issue of 67 uniforms is insufficient to dress all the boys of the school. Other schools are affected similarly.
This situation exists for the following reason: Army headquarters in Ottawa decided that there would be a fixed number of cadets in Canada, (65,000 I believe) and finances are provided to equip and train only that number. This national quota of cadets has not been increased to keep pace with the increased inrolments of the secondary schools in Canada.
Knowing that you are vitally interested in the defence of Canada and knowing that you are aware of the value of cadet training in maintaining this defence, may I suggest that you request the Department of National Defence to have army headquarters increase the national quota of cadets to such a number that all high school boys in Canada can be properly equipped to take the cadet training.
Yours very truly,
(sgd.) G. V. Thornicroft.
I might say that our district is in rather a unique position in that in two world wars we sent many men to the army, navy and air force. We have had a unit in Bruce since
Supply-National Defence the old 32nd regiment was there at the time of the Fenian raids into Canada. But in the reorganization a few years ago our unit was taken away and at the present time our armoury, which was a good one compared with the average, has been sold. In view of the fact that the enrolment in the secondary schools has increased, this principal is not asking for anything out of the way. I know we all agree that cadet training is something that can be very valuable to future service in the army, navy and air force.
I would ask the minister to give consideration to raising the quota. I would not suggest that 100 per cent of all who want to serve should be admitted, but I do say that a quota of 65,000 for the Dominion of Canada at the present time is not large enough.
I might just observe that the ceiling on the number of cadets has recently been raised from 65,000 to 75,000.
That is a little better, but it is still not enough.

Mr. Chairman, the minister mentioned a matter on which I would like to say a few words, namely the selection of the armoured regiment. We have an armoured regiment in my own town of Sussex with which I am sure the minister is familiar. I refer to the Princess Louise Hussars. I doubt whether any regiment in Canada-in fact I know there is no regiment in Canada-has as splendid a record both in war and peace as the Princess Louise Hussars. It has become a yearly habit of theirs to win trophies at camp, both for the quality of their training and also for the number of men they have taken to camp.
This regiment has a very long history. It is one of the oldest regiments in Canada. It was previously a cavalry regiment, organized a good many years ago. It was changed into an armoured regiment just before the second world war. They sent large numbers overseas in the first war; they were overseas in the second war as an armoured unit and gave a splendid account of themselves. They have carried out their training since the reorganization after the second world war.
As I said a moment ago, at Petawawa and in other camps in which this unit has been training every year, they have won practically every trophy which has been given for excellence in training, and I hope when the selection is made the minister will keep in mind what is undoubtedly the best militia armoured unit in Canada today. At the present time this unit is well officered. I know most of the officers; they come from my constituency. The unit has a great tradition and a great record.

Supply-National Defence
I should like to have the minister's attention for a moment because this is a very important matter so far as I am concerned and so far as the unit is concerned. They have a great tradition and a great record. I know of the enthusiasm of the men. I should like the minister to intimate just when the selection will be made and tell us what units are under consideration, or how the selection will be made when it is made.
I cannot think of anything from the point of view of my own peace of mind in the future that would be less desirable for me to say.
I should think it would be a very easy choice.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say one or two words following the remarks made by my colleague the hon. member for Middlesex East, and arising out of the statement the minister gave on June 20 having to do with the reorganization of the auxiliary squadrons of the air force.
At the outset I would like to say I recognize the practical problems which the minister and the department face and faced up to. Certainly we cannot expect to have auxiliary squadrons flying the latest types of aircraft in every small city, town and hamlet across the country and at the same time hope to reduce our defence expenditures. But I would like to reinforce the remarks made by my colleague to the effect, as is no doubt recognized by the minister, that London has been a garrison town for many years, ever since the days of Simcoe and before. Only this past spring the minister himself was invited to be present at an anniversary parade and gathering of a very famous regiment which is one of several with headquarters in London. Just previous to, during and since the last war, the air force came into its own and became a power in the London district. As a matter of fact this airport, which houses auxiliary squadron No. 420, is still the first port of call in Canada of many of the young men who are sent here for air force training by our NATO partners.
I should like to suggest to the minister only one thing. By taking this active flying unit and turning it into a squadron for aircraft control and warning he has done something which if he carries it out, will discourage all those who have participated in the flying training of that squadron, and he will discourage to a great extent the interest of the young people who have grown up in London with the knowledge that at a certain time in their career they could offer their services to that squadron in a flying capacity. Aircraft control and warning, as I think the

minister will agree, is perhaps not the most interesting or enticing type of work to which we can attract the youth of our country who are interested in flying.
I would suggest that one of our greatest needs is transport squadrons. That was recognized by the minister in his speech on June 20, when he announced at page 5210 of Hansard that the Calgary squadron will become a light transport auxiliary squadron. We have the facilities at Crumlin airport to operate a light transport auxiliary squadron. As a matter of fact, the minister will recall certain conversations which have been going on among his department, the Department of Transport and the minister responsible for T.C.A. with respect to that self-same airport. It was as a result of the intervention of the Department of National Defence, in fact, that the runway was extended at some considerable expense to enable 420 squadron to land its T-33 trainer.
I am not going to press for one minute for the continuation of 420 squadron as a jet training squadron, but I suggest it would be most suitable to become a light transport auxiliary squadron, so we can maintain the flying interest that exists in London. The minister is well aware that not many miles to the north there is a regular flying training base to which not only Canadians but persons from all the NATO countries come for their flying training. May I therefore just add my word to the many words that have already been addressed to the minister in the hope that we may retain 420 squadron on some basis as a flying training squadron.

Mr. Chairman, I was disappointed that in his reply the minister did not make any real attempt to meet the criticisms which have been made with regard to the necessity for the reorganization of our forces, and particularly the reorganization of national defence headquarters. I refer to the criticism that it has become a cumbersome, overblown organization which is inefficient and ineffective and would be completely useless to carry out its activities in the event of war.
I do not think that is the case at all.

Earlier today the minister merely said that in his opinion that was not the case. However, it is the opinion of people who should know and who have given evidence in regard to the matter.
As I said earlier, it has been the opinion of every retired senior officer who has served at national defence headquarters since the

war with whom I have talked concerning this matter. I have not spoken to a single retired officer who has served there who did not agree that there is a terrific waste of manpower and a terrific duplication, triplication, quadruplication and multiplication of staffs, with the result that a great deal of paper is simply passed from one department to another. They are kept busy taking in each other's washing. They have indicated it is the type of organization which because of the very form in which it is organized cannot function effectively.
The minister made no effort whatever to meet that criticism. He has not even given us an indication that he would undertake an investigation of defence headquarters with a view to making it a better type of organization. I mentioned five or six instances of triplication or quadruplication of staffs which exist there at the present time, and which I do not believe anybody can defend by saying there is any real need for them. One of these is the medical service, where we have three directorates with a brigadier or the equivalent at the head of each. When we come to the dental service there is only one directorate and one staff instead of three, and they carry on the whole dental service for the three forces quite effectively and efficiently. I see absolutely no reason why the same thing cannot be done as far as the medical and pay services are concerned, as well as the other services I mentioned, which I shall not take time to repeat.
The minister has made no effort whatever to give any answer to the criticism or to give any assurance that a study will be undertaken. When we discussed these estimates before I suggested the possibility of the appointment of a royal commission such as the Otter commission of an earlier day, or the Esher commission in Great Britain, to make a study of the defence set-up and offer recommendations to the government and parliament as to the changes which could be put into effect in order to make a more efficient and better functioning organization.
I strongly deplore the fact that the minister is apparently prepared to let this matter drop. He pays no attention to our requests and disregards the criticism as far as his replies are concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask again if the minister really has nothing to say with regard to what I consider is perhaps the most serious consideration of the 67509-393
Supply-National Defence general national defence set-up and organization at the present time?

Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding the strongly held opinion of my hon. friend, with which I do not agree, I may tell him, if it will help to satisfy him, that the civil side of national defence headquarters is always under study, and if he looks at the figures I think he will see the numbers are down a little this year; not much, but slightly. We have committees studying the matter; we have the civil service commission and the treasury board and our own committee; therefore the civil side is constantly under surveillance. I am just as anxious as the hon. member that we save money without producing inefficiency.
Now, with regard to the service side, the creation of a tri-service group, one group functioning for the three services, is desirable and has every merit but it is not as easy as it sounds, because there are many different factors which obtain in different services in respect of their respective classifications. One of them is in regard to the medical service. We are having studies made concerning this. I do not wish to have the hon. member give the impression to this house and the public that I have no interest in these things. I know they are being studied and that work is being done on them. I do not know how the hon. member can say he knows that what somebody else says is correct and what I say is wrong; I do not know how he arrives at these conclusions. I do say, however, that I feel if national defence headquarters were put to the test, having in mind the quarter of a million people who are more or less under its jurisdiction it would be found adequately and properly set up to meet the test. Perhaps it could take care of its obligations with some fewer people. That is a thing we are always anxious to establish; but I just cannot allow the hon. member to get away with the statement he has made that everything is out of line, because I do not think it is.
Well, Mr. Chairman, all the minister does in this connection is to state his opinion.
All you have been doing is stating your opinion and other people's.

He continues to state his
opinion that everything is all right. Of course I am stating my own opinion and I have been stating it in regard to this matter for years, but I am also stating the opinion of General Simonds, who should know about these things better than anybody else; and his opinion is made quite clear in the articles he has

Supply-National Defence written on the matter. I am stating the opinion, too, of General Macklin, who has also written articles with regard to this matter. I am stating the opinions of a number of retired senior officers who have had considerable experience at national defence headquarters. As I have said, I have not spoken to any one of them who did not hold the opinion I have expressed. Therefore I am prepared to accept that as being the fact rather than accept the opinion of the minister.
In addition I have mentioned half a dozen specific instances to which the minister has been able to make no reply whatever concerning the duplication of staffs and the wastage of manpower and money with the resulting lack of efficiency. For example, there are six chaplains, as I mentioned, with about 240 chaplains to look after; but we have a full colonel and staff for each service in the Protestant and Roman Catholic denominations. Although there are six directorates, I think any reasonable man would say that two would be more than ample.
Concerning the medical services, the minister says there are difficulties in amalgamating them as has been done in the case of the dental services, but we have not heard what the difficulties are and I do not think they would be very great. As a matter of fact, until not very long ago the medical service for the army and the air force was carried on by the army. At one time they were united; then they were split up for no good reason, as far as I have been able to learn. The same thing applies to the pay service and other services. The minister just says that in his opinion there is not much that can be done. That is no answer to these criticisms, and particularly it is not an answer to these specific cases.

Mr. Chairman, might I suggest a specific case where I think amalgamation of the three services could be very easily worked out. That would be the provost corps, where we have provost marshals in the three services and we have shore patrols carrying out the same sort of duty that is carried out by the military police. I suggest to the minister that there is a service where I do not think any serious difficulty would be experienced in bringing about amalgamation.

speechtext:
Do I take it that the committee is agreeable to proceeding to the calling of headings? In order that we may understand the procedure, may I point out that item No. 235 is one item in the estimates and has to be carried or finally disposed of as one item. If it is generally agreed by the committee I shall call each

subheading in the details, and when the discussion on that has been exhausted we shall proceed to the next. After we have gone through all the details item 235 will then be submitted to the committee. Hon. members will find the details commencing on page 305 of the blue book, and I would propose to call each heading and subheading in the order in which they appear. Under defence services the first item is departmental administration.

I notice there is a new
appointment of a superintendent of manpower and establishments with a salary $9,000 per year. Would the minister indicate the duties of this officer, who I presume will be a civilian? While on the question of manpower, because I imagine the superintendent of manpower and establishments will have something to do with the adjustment of the various establishments in the different services, I should like to quote the remarks made yesterday by the minister, as reported on page 6119, of Hansard as follows:
To begin with, a peacetime maximum strength figure is not a target to be reached as an end in itself. Rather, it is a means to an end, a planning limit within which the services agree to work out the details of their programs to enable us successfully to carry out our commitments.
I would assume that in the past agreement was reached among the chiefs of the general staffs in connection with the manpower ceilings, because I presume they would be the only ones who could advise whether the numbers which were authorized would enable them to carry out their commitments. I should like to ask whether it has been the practice in the past to consult the chiefs of staff regarding the ceilings set on the three services, whether this was discussed by the cabinet defence committee when the chiefs of staff were present, and if they gave their concurrence in the decisions reached.

I shall deal first with the position of superintendent of manpower and establishments to which the hon. member referred. This is not an entirely new position, it is a consolidation of two senior administrative positions which were established some years ago. As they were established, one of these positions co-ordinated all matters relating to pay and allowances while the other had to do with the financial aspects of the establishments. One man is now doing these duties which are related to the economic and financial aspect of the manpower employed by the department other than those on the military side. This gentleman is concerned with

ensuring that the ceilings for the use of manpower, particularly civilian manpower, are adequate. He is primarily concerned with the civilian units at headquarters.
He does not deal with the actual military establishment?

No. Dealing with the second question having to do with ceilings and my statement which the hon. member quoted, the ceilings are arrived at, first, by taking cognizance of what we regard as our obligations to NATO, to ourselves, the mobile striking force and various other factors in our defence. The number of people required for the carrying out of these duties is considered and in that connection the chiefs of staff are consulted. There are discussions with them and with departmental officials concerned.
The hon. member will appreciate that each service is anxious to have considerable leeway, and that is the point at which I enter into the picture. We finally arrive at the ceilings. The background behind them is to try to determine-this does not mean that they cannot be changed-the number of people required in each service to fulfil what we consider would be their obligations to the Canadian people, their commitments to NATO and so on. It is the result of a combination of studies. Sometimes there has to be a reconsideration of the over-all picture, but we have not had very much trouble about it. It has been worked out pretty unanimously.

Do I have the minister's
assurance that the final figure reached for the various services would be presented to the chiefs of staff, who would have an opportunity of expressing their opinions to the minister or to the defence committee of cabinet that the figures given were either adequate or inadequate?
Yes.

On page 26 of the white paper, paragraph 89, is to be found the following:
In order to enable station commanders and senior officers to devote more of their time to the operational duties at R.C.A.F. stations, a special administrative course has been organized at London, Ontario, for junior officers.
The University of Western Ontario located at London has a business administration course which is considered one of the finest in Canada, and I am wondering why a special administrative course has been organized by the R.C.A.F. at London. Is that carried on as part of the university work? How many men are attending that course?

I visited London a couple of years ago, and my recollection is that the course is not connected with the university. It is a course especially organized by the R.C.A.F. to meet its needs. I am sorry 1 cannot at the moment give my hon. friend the number of people attending, but when I was there the number was substantial.

Would the
minister look into this and advise me definitely?
Yes.
As the university already has a business administration course I think that should be taken advantage of.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the committee will permit me to read one paragraph of what I said last year when we were discussing defence estimates. I quote from page 4895 of Hansard for June 16, 1955, as follows:
I would think as well that there could be considerable savings in the defence estimates. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich said that at no time did we advocate a cut in defence expenditures at the risk of our national safety, but we appear to be continuing the well-defined program that is ever present in the defence services. In looking over the estimates it would appear we are holding the line on top level appointments, but the empire builders are still at work. The estimates disclose a continual increase in the number of office boys, stenographers, cleaners, helpers, clerks of all grades, chauffeurs and messengers. In one place I even noticed an increase in the helper column from 422 to 1,220.
I think it can be said at this stage that although the minister has indicated that some studies are going on, the reductions are so small they can harilly be found. It would appear that any reductions that are being made in the employment of these categories of persons are taking place in the same places where we are reducing the number of military personnel, and there does not seem to be any indication, on looking through this book for this year, of any type of efficiency examination to see whether the proportion of civilians employed to the number of frontline personnel, if that is what you want to call them, is being reduced.
I am not going to mention at this particular point the places where I checked the numbers and added them up. It is true that there is a decrease in the number of civilians in relation to the army but it is true at the same time that there is a general decrease in the number of personnel in the army. What I would like to know is what type of investigation is taking place within the department to ascertain: (a) whether the greatest efficiency is being attained by the civilians who

Supply-National Defence are working with the military personnel; (b) whether there is duplication of effort in connection with the personnel who are employed; and (c), and I think this is quite important, whether the civilian personnel who are being employed are being given all the necessary equipment to ensure that they can do a good job.
The minister has said that some of these things are matters of opinion, and I am giving him mine. Naturally, until such time as we can have a committee and examine outsiders in connection with these problems, we are all going to be talking opinion and nothing else, but I know for a fact

and I am not going to disclose where you get this information-that there are people in that department who still have to write letters in longhand. Why are they doing so? Because the personnel employed cannot take shorthand. The officers there are writing letters still, in 1956, in longhand and then sending them to somebody to be typed. If that sort of thing is rampant throughout the service, then obviously we are going to continue to have more and more of this type of personnel.
Summing up in connection with this particular item, I say that those three points I have mentioned should form part of the terms of reference of whatever group examines the efficiency standard of the department. In connection with their duties, they should be asking themselves at each stage what does this particular person contribute to increase the efficiency of our national defence? That is, are they filling a role which is going to ensure that the Canadian people generally are better off? r, I am not going to refer to that incident about the dancing classes, but I say that if you are constructing a certain project, if you are going to build a dance hall somewhere-if that may be used as an example- then we are entitled to know what particular function that construction performs in connection with our over-all safety. If you can come back to. us and say it is a question of the morale of the troops, that it is needed for that purpose and that unless you have good morale you cannot have good defence, then you may have a very firm answer; but each expense should be examined on the basis of what contribution it makes to the over-all defence, not to the over-all creation of employment for a great many people with no particular contribution to make.
In closing I should like to ask the minister what does his committee that makes these surveys continually-I think he used the word "continually"-do to see whether improvements can be made? How often do they
fMr. Hamilton (York West! .1
meet, to whom do they report and what have been their recommendations?

The continuing committee consists of a representative of the department, a representative of treasury board and a representative of the civil service commission. They continually assess the material with which they are provided and for which they have asked, the duties and details of organization, and they make their recommendations once a year. I understand that the last complete assessment of national defence was finished in September of last year. They are now engaged on a further study for this year.
I should like to mention one other matter not entirely relevant, perhaps, but I sometimes find it difficult to compare the number of positions year by year. There is a continual change in the nomenclature which I find confusing. I look at one part of the estimates of a particular branch and I find, for example, that last year there were 10 helpers and this year there are 16, and then I find that certain other classes have disappeared. They have been reclassified and this changes the totals of those classes without changing the aggregate. But I feel reasonably assured that the duties that are carried on, on the civilian side-and that is what the hon. member was speaking of- are thoroughly gone over.
The treasury board is very zealous in its efforts to prevent the spending of money. I know that submission after submission that goes from my department-and I understand from other departments, too-to treasury board is referred back for further information, sometimes several times; and sometimes it is turned down completely. They are there for that purpose, and I am not quarrelling with their decisions. Treasury board has a representative dealing with the department, who knows the set-up and the duties people have to carry out in different branches.
Then there is also a member of the civil service commission who is supposed to have expert knowledge of the relative salaries, the duties performed for the salaries and so on. And there is our own representative, who is familiar with the personnel side of the department. That committee is not a rubber-stamp committee in any sense of the word. It works strenuously at its duties and recommends many changes. Sometimes it cuts down staff or recommends reclassifications. What I am trying to say is that the staff is under constant survey.
Is this committee continually sitting? Is it a permanent group? Does it have regular meetings?

I am informed that last year it had between 25 and 30 meetings. Whenever they have material with which they wish to deal and on which they wish to make some decision, a meeting is called. Last year I think there were 27 meetings of this committee. In the meantime their work is going on, material is being provided, questions are being asked, answers are being obtained.

This sounds very much like what I would call a house committee, though not in relation to this chamber. It seems to me that though it may come from various branches of the government, that would be a very appropriate term. Industry today pays a great deal of attention to the calling in of people from outside who they believe can assist in improving their efficiency. As long as this is a house committee, I can see that there may be many things passed over, because of jealousy among various people who are on the committee, that might otherwise be attended to.
Has attention been given to the thought of calling in some outside civilian consultants to look over the efficiency of the department and make recommendations? The reason I ask the question is simply this. You say there is a representative of treasury board on the committee, and that those people are very interested in cutting down total expenditures. That is very fine. On the other hand, they may cut it down on the basis of paying $40 a week to an employee who does not take shorthand instead of paying $50 a week to one who does, and you may end up by having two people at $40 a week doing a job that one at $50 might do. This is not something new. It goes on continually year after year, and I think it might be wise to consult some neutral group and ask them to have a look at the situation in order to see what might be done.

Mr. Chairman, the civil service commission member of this committee has access to all the technical experts of the civil service commission and he is supposed to do what the hon. member has suggested, give expert advice with respect to whether this position should be graded in some other way, whether two jobs should be combined, whether this salary is right, and so on. Throughout the government, of course, the commission has a great mass of information, and that is why it is represented on the committee. The commission is supposed to be the employment counsel of the committee and to make suggestions where it thinks matters could be improved.
