No. I should like to ask the minister to have some of his experts inform us how it is that at the bottom of page 306 we find that this year the following items are identically the same: Civilian allowances, $21,500; travelling and removal expenses, $200,000; freight, express and cartage, $150, and postage, $75,000. There is one item here which is different. The item for professional and special services has been raised from $35,000 to $50,000. What explanation is there for the fact that these items are identical with the previous year's allowances?

I believe there are 22 items at the bottom of page 306 and the top of page 307, and the hon. member has pointed out that most of them are exactly the same. It must be understood that these are estimates. They are based on the average amount spent over a period of time, and particularly on the amount spent during the past year. If the estimate for the past year has been close to the mark the amount is retained. In other cases there have been changes up or down for one reason or another to meet what we anticipate will be the need throughout the year. I will be glad to try to give the hon. member the explanation with respect to any of those items he may wish. There are what we call bread and butter items that occur year after year, and I have the details if the hon. member would like to have them.

So that I may tie this right down and be able to use this as an example, you have a total of 776 personnel this year as against 791 in the previous year. That is a reduction of 15. Yet the travelling expenses are identically the same. What method of calculation, having in mind the difference in the number of personnel, brings you to the same figure?

Frankly, we do not regard the difference between 776 and 791 as of sufficient magnitude to alter the general figure for travelling expenses, unless there is some other reason. These estimates are only general estimates. Every dollar of that item that is spent has to be properly vouchered within the department. If the amount is of any magnitude it has to go to treasury board and it is, of course, subject to internal audit and external audit. The figure that is shown here, being the same as last year, does not mean that with a reduction from 791 to 776 in the personnel we expect that with 15 fewer people the expenses will be exactly the same, certainly not.

Supply-National Defence

Possibly I might be allowed to pursue this, because then I will not have to ask the same question every place it comes up. I want to use this as an example. I referred specifically to this type of thing in my opening remarks, when the estimates were considered previously. Surely in connection with this or any similar figure the ordinary commercial practice in handling a budget for a coming year would be to work out on a per capita basis the average amount which must be set aside, that amount having been proven to have been spent for travel over a period of years. Unless your experts just put down $200,000 and did not use their pencils too freely, surely they would have calculated a per capita amount and come up with some figure like $185,500. If you are running a business on an efficient basis that is the way you would calculate the budget for the coming year.
These lump sums are dumped in here all the way through. They come up not just in this item but time and time again. That is why I ask the question now whether there is any particular reason why the ordinary method of calculating something for a coming year's budget cannot be used here also?

Take the item to which the hon. member referred, travelling and removal expenses. That is set up to cover the travelling and transportation expenses of the minister, the deputy minister and the other departmental administrative staff when they are required to travel. It is broken down into three subitems in the department. Minister, deputy minister and general administrative staff-except audit-is allotted a figure of $50,000. The main item in this amount of $200,000 is for the staff of the chief auditor, and that amount is $134,000. In recent years that amount has been demonstrated as coming pretty close to the mark for him and his staff in doing the travelling audit. Then there is an item of $16,000 for the people of the bureau of current affairs.
Those are the three heads under which this sum is broken down, and the amounts are based on experience. We have to take two things into consideration. The first is the program envisaged in these items, which are all broken down into many subitems. The second is the experience of the past few years. We then take, based on those considerations, a rough figure approximately what is likely to be spent. With the scale of our operations and the complicated nature of our activities, I think it would be pretty much time wasted if we were to try to change this to a figure built up from detailed figures.

In many cases we have a little of the item left over. We try to set up these items so they will approximate what the expenditures are likely to be in the best judgment which the people who make up the estimates can muster. For example, many of these items are more or less constant, but a great many others are not. When we get further along with the items you will see that in the army we rotate a brigade one year and the next year we do not. There are many such factors that enter into some of these items. There are expenditures that recur year after year, and the people who make up the estimates in the first instance have a pretty fair idea of what is likely to be required. They may not get as much as they want, but they tell me first what they think is necessary.

In concluding this subject may I say that I have checked the general expenditure for travel with regard to the army and I notice that it is down from $19 million to $14 million. I suppose we can assume that is because a brigade is not moving at a particular time. However, I think it is safe for us to say that some warning should be given that somewhere along the line these general figures are not going to be acceptable year after year. The minister said that it was a difference between 791 and 776, but if this policy is pursued I assume it will be the same figure next year when it may be 791 as against 750. In other words there must be a tie-in somewhere between the personnel, the jobs they are doing and the amount of money that is set aside for those various items.
I would think we could safely say this, and it has been commented upon by many members in connection with the discussion of the first item; here we have been asked to sign a blank cheque so far as the total amount being spent by this department is concerned. I think it would be reasonable to say that next year when we come back to take another look at these things some consideration should be given to ordinary accounting practices, figuring out your next year's budget and tying that in some way to the numbers you have employed, the types of jobs they are doing and the amount of money you require for this purpose.

In connection with this matter which the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich raised about the director of personnel, which I think the minister said was an amalgamation of two positions which had existed previously-is that correct?
Yes, sir.

In addition, there are directors of personnel for the navy, army and air force. It is one of those cases to which I referred in speaking generally, a quadrupli-cation of effort. In order to try to get at the specific point of view so far as a specific matter is concerned, and to find to what extent they duplicate each other's efforts, I should like to know how much has been charged against each of these four offices during the past year for recruiting purposes. This will, of course, involve a considerable amount which was spent for recruiting during the past fiscal year. How much of that was spent by each of these offices, the director of personnel, which we have just mentioned, and the directors of personnel for the navy, army, and air force.
I am not too clear as to whether the hon. member is dealing with civilian personnel or service personnel?
I am dealing essentially with service personnel. This director of personnel which the minister mentioned deals, he said, with both civilian and service personnel.
No, I said he dealt only with other than service personnel.
I understood you to say he dealt with service personnel.
No, certain personnel on the civilian side; not service personnel.
He has nothing to do with recruiting at all?

Nothing at all. His job is to evaluate the jobs, see that they are being adequately carried out and see that there is no waste effort; that people are working in the field in which they are supposed to be, and so on. It is felt that by combining the two positions to look after the two sides of this matter, the one official can get a better picture of the civilian side. This is purely a civilian matter. I would be glad to deal with the hon. member's question about service personnel when we get to that subject.
I misunderstood the minister. He said "certain" and I thought he said "service". I shall be glad to deal with the question when we come to the military item.
There is a new item, acquisition and construction of buildings, $200,000. Are you building a new headquarters?
Practically all of that sum is for preliminary planning for the new headquarters we hope to build some day.

Have you decided yet on a location?
Supply-National Defence
No; we are labouring on that, and it is considerably mixed up with the green belt at the moment.

No. I wonder if the minister is in a position to answer my question regarding the $2 million expenditure for fire-fighters?

The hon. member asked two questions, and probably I could deal with both of them now. He asked about the junior officers' course at London. I answered part of it, but 1 could not give him the number. Apparently it averages about 40; it does not involve the university. We do, in addition, send one or two senior officers there for special courses each year.
The Department of National Defence fire losses was the other matter about which the hon. member asked. Would the hon. member want to have the figures by years or the average?
By years.
Is there any insurance carried on military establishments?
No, we do not carry insurance.

speechtext: Is departmental administration completed? Inspection services.

I wonder if the minister might outline for us the liaison which exists between this branch of his department and the Department of Defence Production which ordinarily lets the contracts which I assume come under the scrutiny of this inspection service.

The chief of the inspection services, Mr. Chairman, assures me that there is not only complete liaison but continuous liaison between the two at all levels and in all types of work, for the simple reason it has to be so. An inspection takes place of an aeroplane, for instance, that is being constructed, and it has to be acceptable at each step of the work. Our inspection staff, of course, is the group that finally inspects the product we have to pay for and follows the project with the inspectors of defence production.

Supply-National Defence
Who sets the specifications tor the contracts which are required by the department and which are let through the other department?
The Department of National Defence sets the specifications, and then the Department of Defence Production procures, at the cheapest possible cost, materials in accordance with those specifications.

I assume that practically all the work of defence production is tied in with obtaining, facilitating and moving along the contracts for the Department of National Defence. The minister mentioned working with the inspectors of the Department of Defence Production. Is that an indication of duplication, or what particular reason would there be for inspection by defence production and inspection of the same specifications by national defence?

I am in error there. I understand now that our inspectors do all the inspecting, but they work in conjunction with the employees of defence production. So there is no overlapping. Our people do the inspecting.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Inspection services are completed. Royal Canadian Navy, regular force and general.

Is the minister able to answer some of the questions which were put to him regarding the Royal Canadian Navy by the hon. member for Oxford? The questions were of general interest. The hon. member had to go away to another committee this afternoon.

I am sorry but I have not the material to answer these questions offhand. I shall get the answers. A number of them involve considerable detail. If I do not have them ready before the committee deals with this item I shall be glad to see that the hon. member gets them, and anybody else who wishes them. I think there will have to be quite a little searching done to answer some of the questions asked.
The minister would not have the answer to the one regarding the speed of the frigates, which is of very general interest?

I can give some of this information now. It is not quite complete, but it appears to cover most of the points. The original cost of the frigates was approximately $2 million each; that is, for those built during wartime. We do not give out the speed of naval vessels, but frigates have a speed above that of ordinary enemy submarines now in service but probably not above that of the

ones which are just being prototyped. Their engines are reciprocating engines.
As for Tribal destroyers, their life after conversion is estimated to be from six years to 10 years. They were constructed during the period from 1942 to 1947. Each Tribal destroyer cost something over $8 million, about $8,180,000.
The hon. member for Oxford asked about the complement of the Ontario. The complement is 50 officers and 550 men. The average time spent by junior officers training on board the Ontario is three months per year for each cadet, in groups of up to 100 cadets on each trip. There are three cruises a year covering the cadets. The annual cost of operating the Ontario is $2,533,000, including personnel. We expect that of the remainder of the 14 destroyer escorts, the last will be commissioned in 1958. We estimate that their ultimate unit cost, outside of armament and electronic equipment, will be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $17 million each.
To come back to the frigates again, they were all built during world war II and their life expectancy is from six years to eight years. I think that covers the hon. member's questions.

May I ask a question regarding the reserve fleet? What number of vessels have we now in the reserve fleet but not activated and not likely to be activated in the near future, but still kept under a sort of care and maintenance basis?

Page 6 of the white paper sets out the strength of the fleet, both commissioned and in reserve. In reserve there will now be-and it is not shown in the book-one cruiser, the Quebec, six frigates, 21 coastal escorts, five patrol craft, one repair ship, and 63 auxiliaries and small craft.

Is not the number of 21 escort vessels rather excessive? There is a good deal of expense in connection with the maintenance of these vessels in reserve. I understand these escort vessels are not likely to be recommissioned again. Could they be declared as surplus to establishment?

I am informed that the question of the reserve fleet-and I have not included in these figures the three frigates on loan to Norway-is now under study with a view to determining, bearing in mind the cost involved in maintaining the reserve fleet, whether some of them should not be disposed of. We have not as yet come to any conclusion; it is still under study.

I would suggest that these considerations be proceeded with, because

not only do they require a certain amount of maintenance but they also take up a good deal of space in our harbours, and there is no use in keeping them.
Can the minister give a brief description of the cruises which have been undertaken by vessels of the Royal Canadian Navy, because I am of the opinion that those cruises are of very definite value in helping to fight the so-called cold war. Naval vessels go to far-away ports, and from what I know of the ships' companies of these vessels, I am sure they give a good account of themselves.

I am sorry, I have not the particulars of cruises that were made last year. They were fairly numerous. We are not unmindful of the fact the hon. member has mentioned. We wish to keep our ships known on the oceans of the world and in the capitals of other countries. It is just a case of balance as to how many of these cruises should be made, because the cruises are useful for the training of cadets and men. Another thing; if we had too many cruises it might prove too expensive. But we are not unmindful of the fact that it is desirable sometimes to show the flag in other parts of the world.

I think it would be interesting if the minister could at some later time give us that information. I want to ask a question regarding the magazine at Rocky Point. No doubt the minister is expecting me to ask some questions regarding the construction of the jetty at that magazine. I put some questions on the order paper earlier in the session. I was given advice as to the cost of that jetty, which was very considerable.
It was also pointed out in the answer I received that no Canadian naval vessel is capable of berthing at that jetty. All ammunitioning and de-ammunitioning has to be carried out by lighters which have to be brought from the port of Esquimalt, and during stormy weather it is impossible for those lighters to carry out the task they are required to do.
It does seem ridiculous to establish a magazine in which naval ammunition is stored-and the expense of that naval magazine was very heavy, running into millions of dollars, I believe-and not to have a pier or jetty at which naval vessels can tie up and carry out the simple process of ammunitioning or de-ammunitioning. It is almost prehistoric to think of putting ammunition from a vessel into a lighter and then bringing the lighter alongside the jetty and handling the ammunition again. I have seen the jetty myself; it is an expensively constructed jetty with cement piers and that
Supply-National Defence sort of thing. I would ask the minister what are his plans in that respect, and if we are to write it off as simply having been a bad choice of site or bad construction?

Mr. Chairman, the Rocky Point ammunition jetty is not inoperable; it can be tied up to by small vessels. It is not unusable all the time, but under certain weather conditions ammunition has to be handled by lighters.
May I interrupt at this point. From the return I received I learned that no Canadian vessel has ever carried out the task of ammunitioning or de-ammunitioning from the jetty.
The information I have is that it can be done.
But apparently it has not been done yet.

I think the trouble basically arose out of the fact that when the jetty was constructed, it was found for engineering reasons to be so expensive that it was not built to the full length anticipated. Since the ammunition depot has been established the senior officers at Esquimalt have been making a study of the matter. They have evolved several alternatives, and they are making that study with cost figures as well. When that has been completed I shall take a new look at it and so will the officers at headquarters. I think at the moment the situation is substantially as it has been described by the hon. member, but I do not think it can be left in that state.
Does the minister recall the cost of that jetty?

Mr. Chairman, can the minister give the committee details of the transactions within the special account which are expected for this year, the special account being that one which has to do with the transfers under mutual aid?
Perhaps the hon. member would leave that until we get to the army and mutual aid element, because the army accounts for most of the money.

Yes, I
know that; and the air force, too. If I can obtain the answer later on, that will be all right.

A few minutes ago, Mr. Chairman, the minister was giving the facts concerning the destroyer escorts and the light cruisers which I presume are expected to
6198	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence be commissioned sometime in 1958. I would like to ask the minister how many of the 12 destroyer escorts that are being commissioned at the present time are actually operative at the moment?
They are all in commission.

Last year when discussing these estimates the minister indicated that the department was experimenting with helicopters as an anti-submarine scouting weapon. Would the minister care to report whether or not they have been found successful, and what have been the results of those experiments?

A considerable number of experiments have been carried on throughout the past year and they are still being carried on, particularly from smaller ships, which is rather a new departure, so I am able to report that the testing of helicopters for naval operations is going on.
I may say that we also have under way a study with respect to helicopters for the three services in order that we may try to avoid duplication in the services of the same type of helicopter. We are trying to determine in what particular field of each service they can be used. We hope to arrive ultimately at a decision as to how many we should have in each service. Of course in this connection the navy is being given every consideration.
So far, then, you have not come to any definite conclusion as to the value of helicopters as an anti-submarine weapon?
We have not come to any final conclusion, but I think I can say the experiments up to date have been very encouraging and we anticipate there will be a use for them.
Mr. Chairman, a short time ago I think the minister said that the cost of destroyers of the St. Laurent type was $17 million, excluding armament and certain electronic equipment; is that correct?
Yes, sir.

I wonder if the minister could tell us what the armament and electronic equipment will amount to; in other words what will be the total cost? I think that was the question asked by the hon. member for Oxford.
I am informed that the total cost of armament and electronic equipment for the destroyer escorts will be somewhere around $6 million for each.
The total cost will therefore run to $23 million each?
Approximately.

Referring to the matter of the frigates, the minister said they were equipped with reciprocating engines. Are these new engines or the same engines that were in the frigates before, to which certain modifications have been made?
They are the same engines that were originally installed in the vessels. I am informed the theory is that the life of the engines and machinery is usually just about the same as that of the hull.
Is there any possibility of increasing the speed of the engines and thereby increasing the efficiency of the frigates so they would be equal to the task of chasing the most modern Russian submarines?
The question of boosting the engines-I think that is the term used-is one which is under study.
There is some possibility that the speed could be further increased, is that correct?
There is a possibility, but I would not want to hold out that hope because we do not know yet; we have not had our study carried sufficiently far to have determined this fact.

If there is such a possibility I think the situation would be better than it appears to be at the present time, when we have these frigates which will have a life, as I take it from what the minister said, expiring perhaps between 1962 and 1964 or somewhere in that neighbourhood. They have been reconditioned at a cost of between $3 million and $4 million each. It would seem to me if they are not capable of being further increased in speed that has probably been a waste of money to quite an extent.

I am told that the greater part of the cost of modification of the frigates was for new armaments. We must remember that we had to start with what we had in the navy and modernize it, and then work from there into new craft. Most of the money spent on the frigates was spent for armaments and offensive weapons to make them as modern as we could under the circumstances.

I think the situation still exists. It would be somewhat comparable to the air force spending money to modify a Hurricane, which would be a complete waste of money. I do not say that the modification of these frigates is as bad an example as that, but if it is not possible to increase their speed to the point where they can

overtake or at least go as fast as a submarine, it seems to me that we have been sort of throwing good money after bad in modernizing and refitting these ships.

In addition to our obligations to NATO and other obligations, and in order to have our complement filled, it was felt some years ago that it would be desirable to make these changes. I think they are justified, as the ships still have several years of life. It is true they are not the most modern or fastest ships, but at least their equipment and armament is modern.
Are they capable of taking a helicopter on board, or using helicopter as a sort of arm to go out from them for submarine surveys?

Officials of the department are working on one frigate to test the use of helicopters to see whether it will prove effective. There is some doubt as to whether it can be used, but we are going to find out by rule of thumb.
I am glad to hear that that experiment is going on, because that may well justify the expense.

I think the answers we are getting here justify the suspicion of the opposition as to the answers it has had previously. The minister stated there was little reluctance in giving us the answers we want. I understood that the minister's first answer was that these 'ships were fast enough to take care of any present submarine, but that they might not be able to take care of those now under development and being produced. Then later on we got an answer which would indicate that all this is being done to fulfil commitments to NATO. Then we are told that we cannot be given the information as to how fast these ships can go. I think it is fairly well known that if the reciprocating engines are still in them, and I understand they are, they will do about 22 knots. The information to be obtained from Time magazine, if you like- you can get it there when you cannot get it from our department of defence-is that Russian submarines now in operation will do about 25 knots.
I think we are entitled to know if that is the case. As was stated a moment ago, we are spending $3 million or $4 million to modernize these ships. What are we spending it for? Are we spending it to live up to a commitment to NATO to have X number of ships in the Atlantic, or are we spending it to produce something for the defence of this country? That brings me back to my basic remark that for each dollar spent we should
Supply-National Defence have some return. If the figures I have given are not correct we should like to know what they are.
I cannot think of any particular security measure that should prevent us from knowing this. It would not put any prospective opponent in a position to know exactly where we stand. I would be inclined to believe that if other nations knew that this type of engine was still used in these ships, and we were told today that it is, they would know exactly how fast they can go. What is the true situation? Did we spend this money to make it possible for these ships to deal with submarines that we know are in the water now? How long will they be useful? It has been stated here that the natural life of a ship such as this is from six to eight years.

The whole situation is not as simple as my hon. friend claims. We read that the Russians have submarines that will do so many knots, but we can only surmise that that is so. I think we have gone quite a way toward indicating the general condition of the rejuvenated frigates and our various craft. It is not a case of secrecy for secrecy's sake, but I do not think it would be good business to say that we have so many ships which will go so many knots, that we have so many ships of a certain type that will go so many knots, and thus confirm our whole naval picture. I would be really hesitant to do that.
No other nation does that. We have to surmise from the best intelligence we can get just what is the case, and so do they. If I were to state the speed of such and such a ship as it has been rejuvenated I would be providing excellent confirmation. I do not think that is a desirable thing to do. I have tried to give as much information as I could about our naval ships and I have been glad to do that, but I do not think it would be in the best interests of NATO or of our other obligations to give details of the speed and armament of our ships.
We have to be a little careful about things like that. To give that information would be simply confirming beyond peradventure what information other nations may have about these ships. I am not enough of a technical man to say that you can determine the speed of the ship by the fact that it is fitted with reciprocating or some other type of engine. I do not know whether there is a formula that would give that information. I think I have gone quite a way, and I have tried to meet hon. members in regard to the particulars of these ships. I would not care to get into the question of speed.
6200	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence Mr. Hamilton (York West): It seems to me that if we pursue this line continually we are eventually going to arrive at the point where defence will be a matter for the government only and not for parliament. It is just another spoke in the wheel. It simply backs up the argument of the Leader of the Opposition that it is time we had a committee where certain of this information could be obtained which might not be made available in the house. I think the opposition should be placed in possession of information which would indicate whether the money is being spent for useful purposes.
To a great extent these things are generally known. The minister said something about a formula. I am sure if the hon. member for Oxford were here there would be no necessity for a formula. Any officer who had served on one of those ships during the last war and who was told that the same type of engine was being used today would be able to give this information. I realize that the ship has been renovated, and it may be that it can handle second-line submarines, and there must be plenty of them in the ocean. In the case of aircraft, we cannot always have a plane to take care of the fastest bomber, but the fastest bomber is not going to be used in quantity. There will be many secondary bombers which will have to be handled.
I say to the minister what I said last year, that I am extremely disappointed in being able to get many answers out of news magazines published in the United States that apparently I cannot get here. I certainly hope that condition does not continue.

I do not want to get into a controversy about this matter but I would ask the hon. member whether he puts complete credence in the answers on these matters that he reads in United States newspapers, or any newspapers. I am sure those are inaccurate figures in many cases. All kinds of speculation and all kinds of material are published, but the information is not necessarily official and not necessarily correct.
The hon. member made some reference to the fact that apparently the government is the only group that could be fully cognizant of government policy on defence. I do not see how it could be otherwise. The government has to take the responsibility for its policy on defence and it has to be the judge, I should think, of how much information of the type for which the hon. member is asking it is proper to make available. That applies in every country. It may be a disability from the point of view of members, but if we had a committee examining the defence picture, matters of


policy would have to be withdrawn from the committee for reasons which I think are highly justifiable. Otherwise our defence picture in relation to these matters would be an open book, and we would certainly be a unique country if that became the case.

I certainly do not mean to imply that we had a place in the formulation of government policy, but I certainly think we have a place in the approval of the expenditure of these funds. Unless we know exactly what is being accomplished we cannot be expected to vote or not to vote for the appropriation asked for.
All I am saying is that in true cases of security I do not think there is any suggestion from this side that we should know what is going on, but the minister has said, "Don't believe everything you read in these United States publications." I do not think we do, but what is happening there is this. They have a committee in which representatives of the Senate and the House of Representatives have an opportunity of examining these people, and that is where most of the information comes from. It may be that their intelligence is no better than anyone else's and they do not know exactly at what speed Russian submarines can go, but at least they get some information that would enable them to draw a conclusion as to whether in a case like this the money was justified in being spent for this purpose.
The only other thing I should like to ask in connection with these previous questions is this, now that we have found that the cost for destroyers of the new class mentioned totals, I think, $23 million. Are comparable class destroyers being built elsewhere? Have they been designed from the keel up, as I understand these were-and we are properly proud they were designed and built here that way-and have we comparable figures to show whether in this case we are getting value for our dollars in a ship that will do a certain job? I should like to know from the minister whether he knows of any cases like that. If we cannot get the information, it is another argument for a committee to enable us to get it.

I am advised by the naval officials that there are no ships comparable to the new destroyer escort. I am advised that it is the product of a good deal of our own original designing and the best that we could learn from the Americans-as they make their designs available to us-and the British. Out of the three we have built this new destroyer escort which is, we think-

and not only we think, but officials of other countries think-well in advance of anything else now afloat.
I should like to make one other observation about the cost of these destroyers. The hon. member will know very well that the costs of shipbuilding in Canada are very high, relative to the United Kingdom at least and to most other countries, so that, to answer his question shortly, I do not know of any comparable ship against which it could be set in the way of cost.

I should like to say that the picture we have been given this afternoon, as far as the navy is concerned, is pretty bleak. One does not have to read newspaper reports or listen to conjectures or anything else to know that unless these frigates have increased their speed tremendously they cannot possibly cope with any of the more modern submarines or even most of the outdated ones. I can remember very well in the early spring of 1945 listening to one of the ships in our escort group sending back a running account of a chase with a submarine and saying at that time, "We can't shoot it, because we can't catch it." That is exactly the position in which these frigates are at the present time. They have put new armaments in them, new guns, I presume, new depth charges, and so on, but if they can't catch it they can't shoot it. Under those circumstances I cannot see how we could consider those ten frigates as first-line ships by any Stretch of the imagination. That would leave us with one light fleet carrier and 12 destroyer escorts as front-line ships at the present time. In the event of hostilities, if we were given the same job we were given during the last war, that would mean we would have just about enough escort vessels to escort two convoys across the ocean. That is a bleak picture.
I would suggest that, rather than spending $3 million or $4 million in putting new armaments, new depth charges and new guns on outdated, outspeeded frigates, it would be better to try to throw that money into something that could do some good. The frigates, unless the speed has been packed up tremendously, cannot hope even to catch up to a submarine of 1945 vintage, and if they could not do that you can see how far they would be left behind at the present time.
I must say that I was in hopes when I saw this that we at last had a few cruisers, ten frigates and so on to rely on if hostilities should break out, but we are told today that one of the cruisers has been put into mothballs, the other is used as a training ship and
Supply-National Defence ten of the frigates cannot possibly be operational, which leaves us with a grand operational navy of about 13 ships. That is a disheartening thing to have to look at.

I cannot admit that because the frigates cannot overhaul the fastest submarine we know of they are not operational ships. We are working toward a navy where the balance will be in favour of the fastest destroyer which will take care of any submarine that exists. When we get our destroyer escort program finished we shall have 25 destroyers. I do not think any navy in the world has all its navy in first-line ships. It is a progressive growth from one stage to another. These frigates, which had quite a few years of life in them, were refitted so they would be more modernly armed. I think they could play a very useful part in any hostilities that might arise, even though admittedly they probably could not catch the fastest submarine, if we have the right figure as to its speed. However, I think the hon. member is deprecating the picture a little too much.
Perhaps I was minimizing things, but I should hate to be on one.

I should like to refer to two specific matters with respect to the navy item. The first is our shipbuilding program. I appreciate that the Department of Defence Production and also the maritime commission have certain responsibilities in connection with this matter, but I should like to know why it is that our naval construction program cannot be lined up on a year to year basis instead of month to month. We have a shipbuilding industry in Canada, and in the case of the area around Saint John we are dependent on that industry to a large extent. It employs about 1,500 men. This business of handing out contracts every month or two, then causing a serious reduction in employment in the area through cutbacks, and then providing further employment is a drain on the entire community. It may be that some of the larger shipyards do not feel it to the same degree.
I appreciate there are tough decisions that have to be made as far as future plans are concerned, and they have been pointed out this afternoon. But I notice that the minister had this to say, as found at page 6119 of Hansard of yesterday:
There have been no naval developments which were not foreseen reasonably accurately when that figure was agreed on.
He was referring, of course, to the total amount for the navy. I could make a long speech about what I think is wrong with our naval plans. As has been said here and

Supply-National Defence as I mentioned this afternoon, I cannot figure out for the life of me why we are building such a large escort fleet when we have not got a bloody ship to escort. But that is another story. That is a matter of NATO commitments and of what is going to be done with our deplorable merchant marine. I do want to say that we have to line up the plans we are going to make for our navy on a year to year basis, so that contracts will not be handed out piecemeal from month to month.
A destroyer escort or some other small vessel is allocated to a certain shipyard. We have good shipyards and shipbuilders in Canada for a small industry. They complete the project and the job is done satisfactorily. Then the men are laid off, 500, 600 or 700 men on occasion. They wait around and if they are lucky and the lobbying is successful at Ottawa there is another handout next month. The men are rehired, and so the thing goes on. If what the minister says is true, that they can make plans on a year to year basis and there are no substantial changes, then there is something wrong with some department, maybe defence production or the maritime commission. We have to re-examine this matter if we are going to bring about a proper perspective with regard to our plans for naval shipbuilding, something so necessary in the cold war.
I also want to refer briefly to the seaward defences, particularly on the Atlantic coast. I have brought up this subject for the past two or three years and I do not want to go into the details. We do not have too many details. I understand that the plans are pretty well completed at Sydney, and I have read in the white paper this year and in previous years that Halifax and St. John's, Newfoundland, have been considered. I make a plea for the port of Saint John because I think it is one of our major problems today. We have the new Camp Gage-town in that area, a vital new factor from a defensive point of view.
We all know the importance that our ports are beginning to assume in modern warfare.
I have an article here, and there are many others, pointing out the fact that with the modern submarines referred to again this afternoon and the nuclear weapons that will be aboard those submarines, the problem of defending our ports by modern methods has become increasingly serious and important.
I do not have any more to say, but I would appreciate it if the minister would take a moment to comment on the shipbuilding problem and to suggest if there is any way the work can be laid out on a more 

definite basis over the full year, so those who are looking to that industry for their future will be able to make their plans. I should also like him to take a minute to say something about what our plans are going to be for the winter ports on the Atlantic coast.

Before the minister answers that question, may I revert to the problem of the speed of the frigates. We do not have to refer to the United States magazine Life in order to ascertain the speed of the various frigates. I have before me what is recognized by all navies as an official publication, "Jane's Fighting Ships", which gives the speeds of all the vessels of all the different navies, including the frigates about which we have been talking. It also gives the speeds of the submarines and the speeds of various British vessels.
It points out in the foreword that in the case of British navy frigates, ranging from ships of 1,000 tons to 2,000 tons, they have a speed ranging from 16 to 36 knots and widely differing armament. When you turn over the various pages you find a description of the tonnage, armament and speed of the various ships. I think "Jane's Fighting Ships" is considered more reliable than Life. I do not see why the minister needs to be so frightened of that.

I would agree with the
latter statement of my hon. friend, that "Jane's Fighting Ships" is more reliable than Life, but my advisers tell me that nobody would rely on Jane's either; that the figures are very approximate and that they are not technically relied upon by any naval people.
With regard to what the hon. member for Saint John-Albert said, when we decide^ to engage in a shipbuilding program-I am speaking entirely from the point of view of the navy-with the Department of Defence Production we did, as everyone knows, plan our construction in certain yards and certain areas some years ago, and it was proceeded with on that basis and is being completed on that basis.
As far as the navy is concerned, when it comes to repair work that is something that is very uncertain. Except for major overhaul you cannot program it, because you do not know when a destroyer is going to collide with a dock or one ship is going to run into another ship, and so on. There is a great element of uncertainty. In addition, there is the fact that on each coast we have our own dockyards which ordinarily take care of most of the work of maintenance and repair, though not all. When we have a congestion of repair work we utilize the services of private yards.

I am not talking about merchant ships, but of the navy. In the first place there is not a great deal of repair work to do, thinking in terms of the number of yards available; second, it is very hard to program what there is, as there is such a big difference between ship construction and ship repair and maintenance.
