I would crave the indulgence of the committee, Mr. Chairman, to make a few remarks regarding the Canadian army.

Supply-National Defence with particular reference to that portion of the Canadian army which is now serving in Europe. I crave the indulgence of the committee in making these remarks and taking up time, because it is exactly a week ago that I spent the whole day with the Canadian brigade in West Germany.
The first message I should like to bring to the committee is one of which I feel all Canada will be proud. It is a message from the civil authorities of Soest. I met during the evening representatives of the town and the province, and I should like to inform the minister that these civil authorities were loud in their praise of the conduct of our Canadian troops and of the very happy relations which existed between the Canadian armed forces and the civilian population in Westphalia where they are stationed. It is obvious that when troops are stationed in a foreign country many difficult problems are presented, but by the co-operation of the German authorities and the good judgment used by the commanders of our brigade, these little difficulties have been reduced to the very minimum.
Second, I should like to pass on the messages of thanks which were given to me by a senior officer of the newly created German army, who expressed his appreciation of the manner in which the Canadian forces were making available to this army, which is still in the making, their instructors and the advice they might give. We are now working with West Germany as a partner in NATO; therefore it is encouraging to know that old soldiers have been placed on the same side. Officers of the new German army frequent our Canadian messes and discuss their problems as soldiers of armies the world over talk about their kindred problems, which are so similar no matter what nationality the army may represent. Also in that same neighbourhood there are stationed units, in fact a whole division, of the Royal Belgian army, and the same happy relations exist between the Belgians and the Canadians as I have described as existing between the Canadian forces and the German civilian population.
I was asked by representatives of those groups to convey those sentiments to the parliament of Canada and I should like, inadequate though my words may be, to assure the minister that the expressions which were made to me were full of sincerity, and that Canada can be proud of the work her forces are doing in the very difficult circumstances under which they are now soldiering in West Germany.

Then I should like to pay my own tribute to the apparent efficiency of the brigade. I make no apology for saying that our Canadian troops are good. I have been associated with Canadian fighting men all my life, and I know that Canadian troops can be extremely efficient. I am glad to say that our Canadian brigade is well led, that the men are in good heart and well trained, and that the contribution we are making by this brigade group in Western Germany far exceeds the size of the formation for many reasons which I hope to explain later. Not only do Canadians themselves and their commanders consider that they are the very key of the western defences, but that same high regard is held by senior officers of the British and other armies with whom I conversed. I cannot speak in too high terms of the high regard in which our troops in Western Germany are held. There are reasons for that, and I hope I shall be able to explain why it is that our Canadian forces are in such a favourable position.
I do not wish to enumerate particularly the units I saw. Of course I visited my old regiment, the Patricia's, and they were in good heart, but in that brigade there are other units. Unfortunately the Royal Canadian regiment was away on manoeuvres and I was able to see only a very small detachment of them. I did have the privilege of meeting the officers and men of the Royal 22nd regiment, which has a particularly soft spot in my heart. I was closely associated with them during the fighting on the Somme when they gained immortal glory by their attack on the sugar factory at Courcelette, and I had them in my division during the second world war. I was proud to refer to them as my Royal 22nd regiment. They did not have their goat with them, but they had very cherished memories and a very proud and high morale.
After all is said and done, it is the battle honours which are carried on the colours rather than the mascots of a regiment, and it is the names of battalion commanders of bygone days who inspire the esprit de corps of the unit. Names such as Tremblay, Vanier, Percy Flynn, old man Poirier, Bernatchez, Triquet, are household names not only among the Royal 22nd regiment but also throughout the whole of Canada. If by any chance the remarks made from this side of the house earlier today were interpreted as in any way casting any reflection upon the Royal 22nd regiment, I must say that those remarks are not shared by the majority of members on this side of the house or anywhere in the house.

The efficiency of the brigade, which I refer to as being of a very high order, I attribute to certain facts. Remember, they are the only volunteer formation in western Europe, and a volunteer soldier assimilates training more readily than an unwilling soldier who may have been pressed into the service by any form of national conscription. They are also the highest paid troops on the western front. Their units have been maintained at full war strength, with a small reserve immediately to replace casualties. Those are conditions which do not exist amongst the other NATO units which are stationed in the west. The British units are on a lower establishment than our Canadian units. Their units are not even up to the strength of those reduced peacetime establishments, and a high percentage of the men serving in British units are men who perhaps are rather unwilling soldiers, counting the weeks that remain before they will be released to civilian employment.
That is not so with our Canadian soldiers. A high percentage of our Canadian soldiers are men who have served more than one term of enlistment. They apparently are keen on their work and are only too anxious to take part in the numerous exercises which are carried out, and are bursting with pride at being Canadian soldiers.
Regarding the actual quarters and camps in which these men are located, these camps have been constructed, I think I can say, without regard for cost. I do not mean that there may have been unnecessary expenditures, or that care has not been exercised in seeing there was not waste and extravagance. But they are extremely good camps, in which the Canadian soldiers must feel comfortable and at home, and they offer quarters which are in keeping with the type of troops we are sending to Europe.
Of course I may be accused of eulogizing our forces, as has been suggested by some hon. members on the other side of the house. They have expressed surprise that hon. members on this side of the house should compliment or call attention to the efficiency of our troops. I make no apologies for doing this. The only thing I question and call attention to is the fact that if you pay the price you can have practically the best of anything in this world, and Canada has been paying a heavy price for providing the excellent type of troops we have with the splendid facilities they now enjoy.
How long we should continue to keep up this great national effort is something I think the government must take into very serious consideration. There are great expenses connected with the maintenance of that brigade.
Supply-National Defence Not only have we provided excellent unit camps but perhaps I might say extravagant unit camps, extravagant in the extent of ground that the various hutments occupy. A unit camp in West Germany today would be almost comparable in size to a brigade camp during world war II. There are large lawns between the various hutments, and they are kept closely trimmed. Grass grows very quickly in that wet German climate, but the lawns are well cared for by German civilian gardeners whose services are paid for, I presume, by the Canadian forces. There is ample accommodation and no crowding whatever in the hutments.
The married quarters are spacious and the average man in the ranks probably never before lived in such spacious accommodation as he enjoys there. I talked to the wives of some of the private soldiers and they were most enthusiastic regarding the accommodation. They only have to kiep their homes clean. There are no chores to be done around the house, and that presents a little difficulty in connection with some of the growing children, who in Canada would be required to perform certain chores around the house. Those chores are not available to them in Germany because they are all performed by civilian help.
Quarters are provided for the majority of the families and there is an increasing number-one might almost say an incredible number-of children attached to all the various units. Remember, those families and those children are transported from Canada over to Germany and are brought back again. While they are in Germany special arrangements are made to provide them with the kind of food they have here in Canada. Special arrangements are made to import pasteurized milk rather than being required to use the milk which is available locally. Schools are provided, and school teachers are sent to Germany from Canada.
I mention these things because, as I said earlier, we can have the best of everything if we pay the price; and we are paying the price for the accommodation and for transporting and maintaining the families who are now in Europe. I do not know what the actual figure is, but I am going to ask the minister if he will supply this committee with accurate figures regarding the cost of transportation not only of the men, the units and their equipment from Canada to Europe, but also the cost of transporting the families from Canada to West Germany and bringing them back.
I am also going to ask the minister if he can give the committee the figures regarding the cost of either the construction or rental

Supply-National Defence of these various camps in order that we may have some indication of what it is costing the taxpayers of this country to make the contribution to NATO which Canada has been making in the past.
I am not particularly happy about the location of the camps. I do not know whether or not we had any say in the matter. The camps of the brigade are widely distributed. The distance from brigade headquarters to the camp of the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry is something in the nature of 15 miles, and it takes more than an hour to motor from brigade headquarters to that particular unit. That is an indication of the wide distribution which exists amongst the units of the brigade. That scattered distribution may have some advantages, but it certainly increases the difficulties of administration for brigade headquarters, and it also increases the cost.
The area is in a highly developed agricultural district. It consists of a number of small towns and practically every acre is under cultivation, thus restricting the availability of training areas which have to be used not only by our Canadian brigade but also by the Belgian and some British troops, and now the German regiments which are being organized. In fact if the squadron of the armoured regiment wishes to do some tank training the regiment is required to drive its tanks down the road, put them on trains and take them for a considerable distance before they can reach a driving area. The same applies to artillery units and all firing ranges as far as the brigade is concerned.
Those are conditions over which I imagine we had little control. Possibly a few years ago there had not been the development in West Germany that there is today, as many of the present refugees from East Germany had not moved into that area and there was not quite the same demand for housing accommodation that exists today. The demand for housing accommodation by the civilian population has been accentuated by the closing down of several of the rest camps and hostels which were established by the British and United States forces in the area. There is still a steady stream of refugees from East Germany coming into West Germany, and in spite of the tremendous building program which has been carried on there is an acute crowding which is continuously cutting into the training areas and the limited accommodation available for Canadian families who cannot find accommodation in the quarters provided by the government.
These are some of the problems which face the brigade commander, who not only has to train and administer his brigade but must

Supply-National Defence

I should like to thank the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, and I am sure that in doing so I shall be thanking him on behalf of all the members of this house, for the very comprehensive and complete report he has made immediately following his return from visiting Europe on the Canadian brigade located there. I should like to do more than that. I should like to thank him not only on behalf of us in this house but I am sure on behalf of the people of Canada for the very fine tribute he has paid to our troops overseas. As the voice of a very experienced and understanding general who knows something about troops, I think it carries all the more weight. Without labouring the point, I am very grateful to him for all he has said in regard to our troops. I should also like to thank him for conveying to us the views of the German and Belgian civil and military authorities.
After all, NATO is a joint effort. It is the effort of a collection of nations who believe in freedom and are willing to pay a price in an effort to sustain it. I am sure that all the people of this country as well as the members of this house will be grateful for the fact that we know now how well our troops have been received and are being received in Europe.	,
I should also like at this moment to give him such information as I can, as requested in his speech. I have several items here. I have first the cost of rotation of troops, that is the transport of one brigade group over and another brigade group back. For the troops themselves the cost is $2,510,000; for the dependants, $2,652,000, or a total of $5,162,000 for transportation on one rotation over and back.
With regard to married quarters, we have 1,400 married quarters in Germany. These married quarters were built by arrangement with the Germans, who provided the capital. On a long-term arrangement we pay for the use of these quarters $1,185,000 annually in rent, or approximately $65 a month each.
I think that includes lighting and heating too. The rent is paid by the occupant of the premises personally, against allowances which we make. The cost of the construction of these 1,400 married quarters is to be paid through the rent, and the amount I have indicated per year is on the basis of 10 per cent of the capital cost each year.
The other elements in the military camps besides the married quarters are provided by the Germans. They were constructed by them and I suppose that ultimately they will be returned to them in any event if we should withdraw. The over-all cost of operating the brigade group in Germany,


including pay and allowances, food, all the elements that we pay as a government, totals $33 i million per year. I think that covers the figures requested.
Did the minister give the cost of the educational facilities?
I have not the actual figure at hand, but I will try to get it. I suppose the hon. member wants to know the cost of the schools, the teachers, and everything involved?
Yes.
I will try to get that.
Something between 6,000 and 6,500 men, and probably 4,500 dependents.

Did the minister say
6,500?
Between 10,000 and 11,000 with the dependents.
How many of those would be in reserve? That seems a very large number for a brigade. How many would be in reserve?
There are supporting units amounting to 600 or 700 but I understand that the remainder of the 6,000 or 6,500 are all on war establishment and are part of the brigade group.

When I referred to reserves I was referring to the first line reserves which are carried with the unit. Of course there are certain headquarters units which are elsewhere, in Amsterdam and other places. That would appear to be about the figure that one would expect to have, somewhere between
6,000	and 7,000 in a brigade group.
With regard to those persons who are serving in overseas posts, do those who are listed in ancillary positions enjoy the same facilities as those who are in the active force?

I am not sure I clearly understand the question, because once they are sent overseas they are all part of the brigade group. While some might be called ancillary personnel they are part of the brigade group as such, though they may not be what you might call front line fighting troops.
But they still have the same access to accommodation, the same access to all the services which are available to our forces overseas? Is that right?
So far as they are available. I would point out, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich mentioned, that there are not enough married quarters by quite a good deal even with the 1,400.
But how are they divided? Do some people have preference?

The preference is established on the basis of what is called a point score based on the service of the individual, number of children, etc. There is a system of computation on a point basis, and the allocation of married quarters is on that point basis. In other words the greater the claim you have on account of points awarded for length of service and various things the more opportunity you are likely to have to get one of these quarters.
I do not think this is very clear, because the minister has told us that there are between 6,000 and 7,000 persons-
Between 6,000 and 7,000 troops.
All right. What constitutes a brigade; 3,500 to 4,000?

The brigade group, including the first reserves and the ancillary troops, completely absorbs the 6,000 to 6,500 men I have mentioned. They have been permitted to take over their wives and children who constitute approximately 4,000 more persons. Therefore the total brigade group with their dependents runs somewhere between 10,000 and 11,000.

With respect to the 6,500, is there any division made so far as eligibility for accommodation is concerned, or for any other services which are given to our troops overseas, or are they all considered to be members of this group?
Certainly; yes.

To elaborate on that point, perhaps it might be of interest to say that with the exception of the very senior ranks there is no difference in the allocation of quarters for married personnel as between the more or less junior officers, captains and below, and the other ranks.
That is correct.

As a matter of fact, last year when we were overseas I was quite impressed with the accommodation available where married quarters had been supplied. Of course in some places it had not yet been developed, and I would hope that it would develop in very short order. I hope the situation with regard to these people is
Supply-National Defence even better than it was a year ago, but I did wonder whether, within the group mentioned by the minister, there was any differentiation between those who are actually members of the brigade and those who perform ancillary services.

No, I think that distinction does not exist. As outlined by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, with the exception of the very few senior officers the junior officers, non-commissioned officers and men are on an equal basis with regard to claims for accommodation.

That was the impression we received when we were overseas. We saw the facilities which were available for officers of a given rank and below that rank. I may say that one of the things that impressed me overseas was the fact that from a private up to a certain rank of commissioned officer the facilities were the same. Even the furniture which was included in their living quarters was exactly the same. I was quite impressed with that. But that does not alter the question I put to the minister. Is there any differentiation between those who are actually members of the active forces and those who perform ancillary services?

Perhaps the hon. member is thinking of the communications personnel. There are no quarters built for them, and they have to try to get their own. That is not due to their rank or position but due to their location. There are not married quarters for everybody, and they are in groups near places where there is a congestion of troops. There are people who are on lines of communication, you may say, who have to shift for themselves because we do not provide houses in those small areas. That is what the hon. member had in mind?
Yes, thank you very much.

One of the
things I noticed last year when I was visiting Europe with other members of parliament was the obvious lack of news from Canada. It was something which was felt by everybody there. To the people at home perhaps it is not so important, but when you are thousands of miles away you want home news. You want to find out what is going on, whether you live in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto or Montreal. I was told in more than one place that newspapers received from Canada were three to five weeks old.
I do not think that is good enough. I think the provision of adequate, up to date news for the troops is part of the considerations of morale. I realize there is a radio station now in operation, but the radio station does not supply home town news which so many of

Supply-National Defence these men and women crave. What steps have been taken to see that Canadian newspapers are sent to the various areas as rapidly as possible?

On the question of expediting the delivery of newspapers I am afraid I have no up to the minute information. This has been a source of some difficulty everywhere we have had troops. We have tried to take care of some of the difficulty by establishing, as he knows, a new radio station of 250 watts which covers the whole of the brigade area. It gives a continuous series of rebroadcasts from the C.B.C.
That may not meet the local situation of individual troops but I think it is a vast improvement, and has been very well received. I am sorry I cannot tell the hon. member the position with respect to newspapers. I know it has been a perennial headache every time we have sent troops away because it takes so long to get newspapers from here to wherever they are to be delivered. I am very much interested in keeping people away from home still at home in their thinking and their approaches to life. I shall look into that.

May I say
something at this juncture. This business may not loom too large in the minds of many of us here. The minister knows as well as I do that it is a very important thing to the men over there. The provision of this radio station and the excellent programs the C.B.C. are giving do help, but it does not overcome the fact that these men want home town news. The minister may remember that when I returned from Germany I telephoned him and said this was one of the things which were lacking, one of the things the men wanted, and I think they have a right to it. It may be a headache, but I submit the minister might perhaps get some aspirin to restore himself and return refreshed to the task of seeing that these people who are upholding our prestige as Canadians, and who are interested in their home towns, get the news which they so badly need.

I should like to support the hon. member who has just spoken, because it is true that the one complaint we heard was the lack of up to date news from the home towns. Even in cases where members of the forces overseas were receiving their local newspapers as a result of subscriptions, they came in bundles containing the copies for two months at a time. Obviously these men could not begin to digest them. I know that if I am away for a week I cannot begin to read all my home town newspapers for a week, because I just have not the time.


Obviously that is the problem with which these men are faced. Yet they want to know what is going on at home; their ties are at home. They would like to know what has happened, even if it is the accidents on the local streets. They like to read this news. They do not get it until it is quite old, sometimes not for two or three months.
Those of us who were overseas last year found that the main question that was asked of us by the men who were serving from our own home towns was, what has happened at home? What changes have there been? It seems to me there should be some way of getting these newspapers to them within a reasonable length of time, and particularly so when they have subscriptions and are supposed to receive copies by ordinary mail.

There are two points I should like to make in that respect. One is that in a brigade, of course, there are people from every locality in Canada. I do not think there is any particular complaint, at least it has not been brought to my attention if there is, about the general news, especially since we started the radio station. I think the complaints are about their own local news from the little towns and villages. I do not know how the department or the army can expedite that or deal with that, because it is a particularly personal matter.
There are only two ways in which newspapers can be sent to Germany. One is by air and the other is by ship. A ship may be delayed, not I think quite as much as the-hon. member has said, but still there are delays. The cost of sending newspapers by air is rather high for the ordinary family so this is a disability that is very difficult to overcome.
I have said on a number of occasions that the best hope of removing the difficulty is through letters from the people at home to the people overseas, and secondly by sending the local paper to them. I remember that in world war I I got the local paper every week, except when I got lost upon occasion. It was a local paper and was not of any interest to anybody else so far as I know. But it was of interest to me. I think it should be pointed out that the families who have someone overseas might very well develop some sense of responsibility for keeping that individual informed. I believe, taking that with the general information we are able to give them, plus the radio service we are able to provide, should meet the situation.
I agree there is quite a bit of complaint about it, but I do not see how the army itself could meet this particular situation without.

the co-operation of the relatives and friends of the people who are in the services.

That is the very thing 1 am talking about, Mr. Chairman. In several cases which were drawn to my attention those people who were subscribers to local newspapers did not receive those newspapers because they went, I suppose, as newspaper mail; I do not know how they got them, but they were getting bundles of newspapers at one time which were anything up to a month or two months old. They had no news in the meantime, yet they had subscribed to that newspaper. It seems to me there must be some things the department could do to see that this second or third class mail reaches them in a reasonable length of time.

I am told by the postal
people that the average transportation time for air mail to the brigade-
That is air mail, though.

I will give you both-from Montreal to the brigade is three to four days. The average time for surface mail is from 12 to 18 days. There may be some delays, but generally speaking that is about the time that can be counted upon.
There is another thing-I do not suppose this meets the local situation-but I know when I was last over there a great many of the units whose men came from certain areas subscribed to a number of papers from that area and they were used by all members of the units. In other words there are the costs, and so on. I am very cognizant of the situation, but I do not think there is really very much more we can do than we have done to expedite things.

Perhaps I might say a word on this subject. When I was over and saw the brigade and the air division last year the only complaint I heard, I think, in connection with this matter was the lack of news. The radio station will no doubt have corrected that to some extent as far as the brigade is concerned; it will not have corrected it as far as the air division is concerned.
The minister has said he does not think there is anything further the army could do, and I take that to mean anything the department could do. I think there is. As a matter of fact I asked two or three commanding officers whether it would help, or be of any particular assistance, if newspapers from the home station of the unit were flown over as part of the regular cargo of the skid run, I think it is called, of the air force which goes over, I think, twice a week or something
Supply-National Defence along that line. They were of the opinion that it would be of very considerable assistance.
An artillery regiment which was there at that time, for example, came from Winnipeg, or that was its home station, and they considered that if they got four copies of the two Winnipeg papers in their regular delivery by the air force scheduled run, two for the men's mess, one for the N.C.O.'s mess and one for the officers' mess, it would be of very considerable importance and would help the situation materially. The same thing would apply as far as the P.P.C.L.I. is concerned whose home station at the time was Calgary, and the same would apply to other units. It does seem to me that the department could ameliorate this situation without any undue cost by that particular means.

I do not know, Mr. Chairman, that the newspapers from the home stations of the units would be enough, because I think what the members of those units are concerned about are their home towns. This has been looked into, but I shall be glad to have it looked into again. The difficulty, I think, really arose, when I looked at it last time, and when we canvassed the areas of the different units very thoroughly, especially in regard to daily papers. We found that the weight was a formidable barrier expense wise. On the scheduled run we have to be very careful with our space. However, I shall be very glad to have it looked at again.

As the minister said, if you had to send a newspaper to every man over there obviously you just could not do it; but if you tried to send, as the hon. member for Calgary North said, a couple of newspapers or four newspapers from each major centre from which the men come it would help. The units that are overseas have headquarters; they have a domicile in Canada, and if you tried to provide them with the newspapers from the Canadian domicile of their units it would at least ameliorate the situation to some extent.

Mr. Chairman, I want to revert to the question of married quarters. On page 28 of the white paper is given a summary of the situation with regard to married quarters. As of December 31, 1955, we are given a total of 30,000 married quarters, of which 3,217 are for personnel in Europe. I think the figure the minister gave was 1,400. I suppose the remainder is made up of married quarters for the air force, and the number under construction or in the planning stage. What I should like to know is, during the current year roughly how many additional married quarters will be available in Europe?

Supply-National Defence

The difference is, of course, as the hon. member says in Grostenquin and Marville, in France, and Zweibrucken and Soest in Germany. I understand that all the married quarters contemplated in Europe will be completed this year.

There are two other questions which I propose to ask. I notice recently there has been a competition advertised for what seems to me a large number of vacancies on the staff at the Royal Military College at Kingston. What is the explanation? Is there an addition to the staff, or has there been considerable rotation of the staff? Perhaps the minister can give some indication of the total number of positions. These are civilian positions. One came in today from the civil service commission. I am wondering whether these are additions to the staff or replacements for professors who have resigned their positions.
I have another question that I should ask while the minister is finding the answer to the last one. I notice at page 20 of the white paper is given a summary of the number of civilians employed by the armed services in the different categories. I wonder what the explanation is as to why the army seems to employ a much higher percentage of civilians than either of the other services? In the classified bracket the army employs over 12,000 civilians against the air forces under 8,000, although the strength of the air force is actually greater.

Dealing with the first question raised by the hon. member, the number of professors at the Royal Military College has been increased by two, so to that extent they are new appointments. Altogether I think there are over 40 professors and the number has been increased this year by two. Therefore the applications mentioned by the hon. member, except so far as they refer to these two, would be replacements. I think it is quite common in academic circles for civilian professors and lecturers to move about fairly often to different positions, and I think that is exactly what has happened at R.M.C.

I notice that at page 319 of the explanation of the estimates reference is made to professors, assistant professors and lecturers at the Royal Military College. What about the professors and assistant professors at Saint Jean, Quebec? Where are they included?

They will be shown in the air force section when we come to it. They are tri-service colleges. Royal Roads is operated by the navy. R.M.C. is operated by the army and C.M.R. is operated by the air force.
Is the majority of students at Saint Jean army students?
They are all tri-service colleges. The administration of each college is given to one service: Royal Roads to the navy, R.M.C. to the army, and C.M.R. to the air force.

I wonder
whether we might go back to the question of the dependents who are overseas with the brigade. I think the minister said that probably about 4,500 people are there, and some concern has been expressed about their being over there from the standpoint of their own safety. I think we are all very glad that they are there and I am quite sure it contributes greatly to the morale of the brigade, but I am wondering what type of program the department has for the evacuation of those people in a time of crisis? Have we the necessary shipping laid on? Is there a crash program to insure that these people are evacuated immediately? Otherwise it would appear they would only contribute to a great deal of confusion at a very vital part of the campaign.

This, of course, is primarily a NATO problem and one that has not been completely solved. During the past year, and ever since I became minister of this department some quite extensive studies have been going on, and in that connection we are working with other departments in an effort to set up a procedure and a policy to be followed in the event that evacuation becomes necessary.
I may say we have not come to any final conclusions. This is quite a difficult problem, as the hon. member will realize, but it is a problem I think we have to continue to consider until we reach what we believe is a satisfactory solution. I am sure that in the end we will reach a conclusion, but we have not as yet because the studies are not completed.

I think this is probably the most important point in connection with the whole procedure of having dependents overseas, that is outside of the morale question in relation to the troops. I understand that we take them over there and assume the responsibility for their transportation there and back during ordinary times. Surely we are not going to fall back on some type of NATO program for these people in a time of emergency.
It would seem to me, sir, the very least the department should know at this time is the port of embarkation and the availability of shipping. It seems to me that the brigade and their dependents have been over there

for a sufficient length of time for a program covering their evacuation to have been mapped out. I would think the minister's statement will leave a lot of uneasy minds in Canada when it is read.

If we have a reasonable period of warning that is, notice of ten days or so, our program is worked out. But if it is a sudden thing that might come out of the night there are problems which have not been completely settled. For example, the hon. member says we ought to know what port will be used. We do not know what ports will exist following a sudden attack. Shipping will depend on the ports that are available to us. This raises very grave and difficult problems, because there cannot be any certainty in the process of evacuation. We are trying to work out alternatives and a scheme of things that will take care of any situation. I hope we shall have reached final conclusions before too long but, as I said, we have reached the point where if we have some reasonable notice I think we can handle the situation, but we are not yet at the point where we can say it is complete.

May I suggest that the minister certainly seems to be grasping the point in connection with this question. I think he might put some of his experts to work in connection with this important problem, because it appears to me to be extremely urgent. If we are going to go along without having a program lined up then I think the dependents of these people and their relatives here should be made well aware before they leave that there is no concrete program for them in connection with their return.
If I may remain on my feet, Mr. Chairman, because it is extremely difficult to get here in the first place, I should like to raise another point. I am wondering if the experts in the department have made any decision, as has been done in the United States, concerning which branch of the service will handle the intercontinental guided missile if and when it is available to our forces, and the intermediate range ballistic missile.
Perhaps it is because of differences of opinion in the services and because of an attempt in the United States to settle this, but I understand in that country the intermediate range ballistic missile has been handed over to the army for development and use and the intercontinental guided missile has been handed over to the air force for development and use. If we are properly planning for the future it seems to me there 67509-394
Supply-National Defence should be a decision at an early date in connection with the use of those weapons if a decision has not already been reached. I think we are entitled to know from a policy standpoint what is going to be done in this country concerning those weapons.

Well, Mr. Chairman, the question of ground to air guided missiles other than in an experimental sense has not yet arisen in Canada. We are studying ground to air missiles, but we have not yet committed ourselves to any, so we have no definite program as to which service will deal with them when we do have them. Concerning the question of air to air guided missiles, there is the "Sparrow" to which we are committed, and that is in the jurisdiction of the R.C.A.F.
As far as the intercontinental guided ballistic missile is concerned, I am one of those who think it is very far in the future, and it is not within our purview to deal with any particular one at the moment. So I would not hazard a guess with respect to who would look after it. There will not be anyone who will care to look after it, I fear.

In connection with the intermediate range guided ballistic missile, have we had any technicians attached to the United States forces to study their developments in that country, and have we made any progress in determining whether our artillery or air force will be using these weapons? It seems to me these are questions that should be answered at this time. If we are attempting to keep abreast of developments, I think in co-operation with the United States forces we should have men there on the ground today learning the use of these weapons and the technical features of their development in order that we will be abreast of everything that is new.

As the hon. member will know, in the way of ground to air missiles there is the Nike and the air force has air to air missiles but, as I say, the intercontinental guided ballistic missile, whether intermediate or final, is quite a long way in the future. I think we have ample time before it becomes fully developed in spite of what is said by certain newspaper columnists.
I wonder if I might now fulfil an undertaking I gave to the hon. member for Winnipeg North with regard to the question he raised concerning the special account. He referred to the special account item listed on page 318 of the blue book as item 34 under the navy estimates, where there is a nil entry for this year. The same account also appears on page 331 under the army estimates and the reason item 34 of the air force estimates

Supply-National Defence on page 338 does not include a reference to special accounts will become evident from what I have to say in a moment.
In the past year the value of equipment acquired to March 31, 1950, that has been given as mutual aid to our NATO partners has been credited to this special account for procuring more modem equipment for the Canadian forces. Since April 1, 1956, no further credits will be made to this account and at that time the credit balance stood at $281,933,743. I think I may take some credit or blame as the case may be for that decision, because I do not like carrying these things along from year to year and complicating the ordinary accounting system. The only charge to this special account proposed for the fiscal year 1956-57 is $72,141,000 by the army.
There are relatively small quantities of equipment remaining in Canadian stocks that were acquired prior to March 31, 1950, and where such equipment is transferred in future it will be valued for mutual aid purposes at approximately the cost of repairing and shipping. Consequently these transactions will be on a current disbursement basis, and the charge to mutual aid will be deducted from the expenditures of the service that incurs them rather than credited to the special account.
What is going to happen to the surplus in that special account?
We are running it down by $72 million this year. In other words it will not grow; it will be run down on the usual basis until it disappears.
In other words it is being used to supply new equipment to the services?
That is right.

How much money has been expended already on the Gagetown camp? How soon is it expected to have the camp completed? How many accounts in connection with land taken over by the department are still unsettled?
I had better have my figures checked before I answer. I shall get the information and give it to my hon. friend.

The minister told us earlier that we should not place too much reliance on press reports, so perhaps the minister will give us a statement with regard to the manufacture of the Belgian rifle and bring us up to date on the program.

The contract for the production of the FN-C1 rifle, as we call it with our modification, was awarded by the Department
[Mr. Campney.)
of Defence Production to Canadian Arsenals Limited in September, 1955. Tooling has now been virtually completed and the purchasing of all production materials is now well advanced. Deliveries are expected to commence in the autumn of this year. Based on the above forecast of production it is anticipated that sufficient rifles and ammunition will be available to permit introduction into the Canadian army as follows: To the Canadian army, regular, between May, 1957 and July, 1958; to the Canadian army, militia, between July, 1959 and January, 1960.
I assume ammunition for that rifle is in production now?
Yes, it is.

According to a press report I have here it is estimated that 72,000 of these rifles are to be produced for Canada, and I should like to know what will be done with the Lee Enfield rifles which will be replaced.
No specific decision has been taken with regard to them, but of course they might become valuable for mutual aid if any country should want them, or they could be disposed of in some other way.

I hope the department will not forget what happened in 1940 after Dunkirk, when rifles were in such short supply in all the western nations, and will keep a sufficient quantity of Lee Enfield rifles in store for emergency use. I hope they will not end up in the crown assets corporation and finally go on the international market as sports rifles.

I note on page 326 of the details under "Major procurement of equipment" an item covering tanks and armoured fighting vehicles, where the amount this year is $590,000 as compared with $5,769,000 last year. This is a great reduction in the amount for tanks and armoured fighting vehicles, and is hardly in accord with the minister's announcement that a new armoured regiment was to be constituted and that the army was to be supplied with a considerable number of amphibious armoured vehicles which could be used for a variety of purposes. I wonder if the minister would explain this apparent discrepancy between that announcement and the amount of money being voted for armoured fighting vehicles.

I am informed that we have available enough tanks to equip the new armoured regiment except for some minor parts, and therefore further purchases are not necessary. I did not get the second part of the hon. member's question.
The minister announced that amphibious armoured vehicles would be used for a variety of purposes, and I presume they would come under this item.

I think the hon. member is referring to the same vehicles to which I referred this afternoon. I said that we were approaching the prototype stage of development, but the vehicle is not in operational production.
In other words, it is not anticipated that any of these vehicles will be completed during this fiscal year?
We hope to have a number of the prototypes during this fiscal year.

I am rather disappointed, because when the minister made his initial statement with regard to these particular vehicles I understood him to say that they would be in the course of being supplied to the Canadian army during the present year.
I did not say that.

The minister says that he did not say that, but he certainly left that impression with me and I would think with the majority of his listeners. The minister has said that there are enough tanks on hand to supply the new armoured regiment which is going to be constituted. I wonder if he can tell us how many extras that will leave to replace the casualties which constantly occur in the use of tanks, in the same way as automobiles are constantly being piled up on the highways. Furthermore, what about the reserve army as far as the supply of Centurion tanks is concerned, which I understood was to go forward?

I understand from my officials, as I have said, that we have an adequate number of Centurions to equip the regular army with a sufficient reserve for an appreciable time if they were called into service, but there are not on hand at the moment a sufficient number of these tanks for the militia.
Can the minister give any indication how soon the militia armoured regiments may expect to receive a sufficient number of Centurion tanks with which to carry on training?
No, I am sorry that I cannot at this moment give any date.

Is there any hope of having these vehicles within the next year or two? In some cases these regiments are getting a little fed up over the lack of equipment and with what you might call continued promises, which are not met, that they will be supplied with this modern equipment.
Supply-National Defence

I am sorry, but I cannot give the hon. member any data. I understand that the militia units are fairly well equipped with Sherman tanks, but there are no figures I can give him with respect to the Centurion.
Could the minister give me the information I asked for?

I waited so long that somebody got in ahead of me with the same question, but there is one further question. I notice an increase from $1,900,000 to $2,500,000 for architects, engineers, land valuation and legal fees. Is there any particular reason for that increase this year? That is on page 325.

Apparently the work of this particular branch, architects and engineers, has lagged behind. I might interject that this is administered by Defence Construction Limited. The estimate for the current year was prepared before we realized last fall that the figure was low and would not be adequate, and the additional sum of $600,000 was put in to cover what we estimated would be the eventual requirements beyond the original estimate.

I do not think that answers anything. Is there any particular special project in any of the four categories mentioned that requires an additional $600,000? Perhaps the minister might tell us what method is used to pay these people. Are these evaluators on contracts of some kind? Are they individually employed in the various districts, and if it is for legal fees what special project is involved? I think we should know that.

These are consultants who are hired by Defence Construction Limited for our account. I might say that in the last two years we have instituted a small branch in the department to correlate and further our construction program. It has been very successful, and it has had three results. In the first place we have had far less replanning and changing than was formerly the case. In the second place it has meant planning further ahead than was heretofore possible. In the third place, and probably partly as a result of the two factors I have mentioned, in the current year construction has been stepped up very materially. Whenever construction grows in volume we naturally have to have more architects, legal people and consultants. I think it is also directly as a result of the changes we have made, which have been very effective in these other particulars.

Supply-National Defence
I expect that in future years, if this is to take care of a more prolonged program, this item should not be jumping again by $600,000.
I should not think so.

I notice that armament equipment has increased from $7,760,000 to $10,227,000. I wonder whether the minister could indicate to us briefly what that increase is intended to cover in the way of armaments.

This increase is attributable principally to the introduction of the new rifle, which is to be produced in Canada, the tooling and commencement of production, and also to the deliveries of 105 millimeter howitzers for which we have provided funds.
I do not think the minister finished giving his answer. He said that money was provided for 105 millimeter guns but he did not say what it was.
The figure with respect to the 105 millimeter howitzers is $3 million in this vote, and with respect to the FN rifle it is $2| million.
In other words, the other $5 million is more or less for replacements?
Yes.
Could the minister tell us how much the department is paying for these 105 millimeter guns?
That probably could be answered by my colleague the Minister of Defence Production, when his estimates come up. I did know the price, but I do not recall it now, and I would not care to guess.
Does the minister know how many guns he got for the $3 million?
We do not give out figures as to quantities of armaments. We never have, and I do not think we should start that now.

I do not think that answer is very satisfactory. As a matter of fact we have mentioned a number of guns of various kinds on frequent occasions, both here and in the defence expenditures committee, and I would ask the minister to what extent the Canadian army has been rearmed with 105 millimeter guns.
The regular army has been fully rearmed with these guns. These are for the militia.
To what extent is the militia being rearmed with these 105 millimeter guns?
We hope eventually completely, but this is a start in that direction.
Then might I ask how many guns per militia regiment have now gone out?
As far as I know none of them have gone out.
That is my information, that none have gone out; but the minister says these guns are for the militia regiments.
They are being purchased. They are being built for that purpose, but they are not yet available.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They have not been built yet.
May I ask once more how many are going to be supplied to each militia regiment, and how soon?

I understand that the scale is about eight per regiment. I certainly cannot give the date for the production of the guns. I would not give a date of production of anything after two years in this department, because there are all kinds of production problems, and we are now in the middle of a steel strike.

This great reluctance or inability on the part of the minister to give such information as how many guns are covered by this $3 million order, on the basis that it would break security to give it, is a good example of how little necessity there is for security of that sort, because the number of field regiments in Canada is quite well known. It is published in various publications, and anybody can get the information. If these guns are being purchased for the militia regiments on the basis of eight for each, no consideration of security enters into the matter at all.
I think this is a good example of the fact that we have been denied information very frequently in this committee, in the defence expenditures committee and in other places as far as defence matters are concerned on the excuse of security, when there was no real security reason whatever. It was either the fact that the people concerned .did not have the information or they were afraid to give it because they thought there might be some unfortunate consequence politically from doing so.
I asked the minister several questions with reference to Camp Gagetown and he said he would have the information.

The information has not yet come to hand, but I have not forgotten it.

I can assure the hon. member he will have it, but I do not know that I will have it before ten o'clock.
I want the committee to have it.
I asked the minister for an explanation, and perhaps he has it now, of why the proportion of civilians to servicemen is so much higher in the army than in the other two services.

I am told that one of the
principal reasons the number of civilians in the army is higher than in the other two services is the type of work for which they are used. For example, the transport situation is far greater in the army than in the other two services and a much larger civilian staff can be employed to service vehicles. The same applies to ordnance. Much of our R.C.A.F. repair work is done by the aircraft industry. To put it shortly, a great deal more maintenance and repair work can be done by civilians in connection with army operations than in the other two services. It is cheaper to do it that way and equally effective, and in the interests of economy we try to use civilians wherever practicable.

I should like to ask the minister a question which, while it affects comparatively few men in the regular force, is of great importance to them. He will remember that two or three years ago there was one regular battalion made up of four highland companies. One of these companies was from Vancouver, the Seaforth Highlanders. For some reason or other a change was made and the whole battalion was converted into a Black Watch battalion rather than a Seaforth battalion, which I think should have been done.
However, the young officers from the Sea-forths were compelled to buy completely new highland outfits with the Black Watch tartan. Unless it has been done recently, I believe no help has been given them to meet that expense. In view of the fact that they were forced to get these new uniforms I suggest that they should at least have been given some allowance by the army to help with the purchase of the uniforms.

I may say that I am entirely sympathetic with the hon. member in this matter. I made two different submissions to treasury board, and I am not sure whether there may not have been more. I do not want to shove the matter off on treasury board, but I must exonerate myself. I have not the power to take the remedial action that I think should be taken. The members of treasury board have different views, as they have a right to have, but I agree with the hon. member. These changes having
Supply-National Defence been made in the natural course of evolution of the army and through no fault of these personnel, I believe there should be some assistance. But I must admit that up to now I have not been able to get a satisfactory solution.

Has that suggestion been turned down by treasury board? If so, will the minister again place it before treasury board; because I think here is a case where, since there are so few men involved, treasury board is not being fair. These young men have a good claim for help in the purchase of these expensive uniforms. I hope the minister will again put the case before treasury board and that this time the suggestion will be met. Can the minister give the committee the assurance that he will again take it up with treasury board?
Yes, I will be glad to do that because, as I say, there is no difference in our opinions on this matter.

speechtext: Does that complete the discussion under this heading?

I was amazed at the answer given by the minister to the question asked him by the member for York West about the evacuation plan for the relatives of married personnel in Europe. Perhaps I did not understand what the minister said. Would he explain just what the plan of evacuation is in case the balloon goes up over there? How are these people to get out in safety?

If I may repeat, these matters are under consideration not only by us but by the NATO authorities and by other departments. I think I am right in saying that such matters are not publicized, that no publicity is given to what plans we may have in mind or maybe trying to evolve. It is of course, as everyone knows, a very important matter. I do not know that any good purpose would be served by discussing publicly the plans that have so far been evolved nor, in fact, the plans when they are finalized.
Why does the minister not say there are no plans and cut it short?
Because that would not be in accordance with the facts.
Is there a plan? I am not asking what it is. I want to know if there is a plan or if there is not a plan.

I answered the question before the hon. member came in. I said the plan had been evolved to a certain point. I was asked whether the ports of debarkation and the methods of assigning those ports had been settled and I said no. I said there

Supply-National Defence were a number of problems in connection with evacuation that had not yet been settled. I said that plans had been partially formulated but not completed.

How long does it take for the government or this department to work out plans for a brigade that has been in Europe a number of years? Is it going to take another two or three years before you finally get a plan worked out? Just what is the process of the department's thinking? How much more thinking has been done during the past year than the year before, and when do you expect to have a plan worked out?
Ten o'clock.
All right, we will call it ten o'clock.

The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Have tenders been called for construction of
Question
a new Royal Canadian Mounted Police detachment building at Amherst, Nova Scotia?
